Three bare "without" clauses, each naming a thing the cultivated person cannot do without: ming, the ordinances or mandate of Heaven (the same word that opens this very book in Yao's charge); li, plain "ritual" as throughout this edition (Legge's "rules of Propriety"); and yan, words — the power to weigh what people say and so to know them. We hold the three in matched, unpadded clauses, junzi as "cultivated person" and li as "ritual" to keep the house terms steady to the final line, and let "to know people" close the book on the note the Analects has sounded from the first: that all of this learning is, in the end, about knowing and becoming fully human.

segments.text: The Master said, "To learn, and in good time to practice what you have learned — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from far away — is that not a joy? To go unrecognized and feel no bitterness — is that not a gentleman?"

The Master said: To learn something, and then in good time to practice it — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from distant places — is that not a joy? To go unrecognized by others and yet feel no resentment — is that not the mark of a fully realized person?

Master Yu said, "Men who honor their parents and respect their elder brothers rarely have a taste for defying their superiors, and no man without that taste has ever been fond of stirring up revolt. The gentleman tends to the root; when the root is set, the Way grows from it. Devotion to parents and respect for elders — surely these are the root of human-heartedness."

Master Yu said: A man who is good to his parents and his elders is rarely the kind who defies those above him; and a man who does not defy those above him is never the kind who stirs up rebellion. The cultivated person tends to the root, for once the root is firm, the way grows up from it. Devotion to parents and respect for elders — surely these are the root of humaneness.
The Master said, "Clever words and a winning face rarely keep company with human-heartedness."
The Master said: Fine words and a fawning face are seldom found together with humaneness.
Master Tsang said, "Each day I examine myself on three points. Working for others, was I faithless? With my friends, did I fail to keep my word? What was handed on to me, did I leave unpracticed?"

Master Tsang said: Each day I examine myself on three points. In handling another's affairs, have I been less than faithful? In dealings with friends, have I been less than sincere? And what my teacher passed on to me — have I failed to make it my own and put it into practice?
The Master said, "To govern a state of a thousand chariots: attend to the work and keep your word; spend little and love the people; and call on their labor only in the right season."

The Master said: To govern a state of a thousand chariots, attend reverently to its business and keep your word; be sparing in spending and care for the people; and call on them for labor only at the proper seasons.

The Master said, "A young man should be devoted to his parents at home and respectful to his elders away from it. He should be careful and truthful, love everyone, and keep close to the human-hearted. If he has strength left after that, let him spend it on study."

The Master said: At home a young man should be good to his parents; abroad, respectful to his elders. He should be careful and trustworthy, overflow with love for all, and keep close to those who are humane. If after all this he has energy to spare, let him spend it on study.

Tsze-hsia said, "A man who prizes worth over beauty, who serves his parents with all his strength, who would give his life for his prince, and whose word to his friends is good — others may say he is unlearned; I will call him learned."

Tsze-hsia said: A man who prizes character as much as most men prize a beautiful face; who serves his parents with all his strength, and his ruler with his very life; who is true to his word among his friends — though others may say he has had no learning, I would call him learned indeed.

The Master said, "A gentleman without gravity carries no weight, and his learning does not hold. Put faithfulness and keeping your word first. Have no friends who are not your equals. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to change."

The Master said: If a leader has no weight, he commands no respect, and his learning will not be solid. Hold faithfulness and sincerity above all. Take no friend who is not your equal in this. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to set it right.
Master Tsang said, "Give the dead their full rites, and keep the long-departed in remembrance, and the virtue of the people will grow deep again."
Master Tsang said: Tend carefully to the rites for parents at their death, and keep up the sacrifices long after they are gone — then the character of the people will be restored to its full worth.

Tsze-ch'in asked Tsze-kung, "Wherever our master goes, he learns everything about how the place is governed. Does he ask for it, or is it offered?" Tsze-kung said, "Our master gets it by being warm, upright, courteous, temperate, and deferential. His way of asking is not other men's way of asking."

Tsze-ch'in asked Tsze-kung: Whenever the Master arrives in a country, he always learns how it is governed. Does he ask for this, or is it offered to him? Tsze-kung said: The Master gets it by being gentle, honest, courteous, modest, and yielding. His way of seeking it is surely not the way of other men.

The Master said, "While a man's father lives, watch what he means to do. When his father dies, watch what he does. If for three years he does not turn from his father's way, he may be called a devoted son."
The Master said: While his father is alive, watch the son's intentions; once his father is dead, watch his conduct. If for three years he keeps to his father's ways, he may be called a devoted son.

Master Yu said, "In the practice of ritual, ease is the thing to prize. This was the beauty of the way of the ancient kings; in matters small and great, they followed it. But there is a limit. To know the worth of ease and be easy, without ritual to give it shape — that will not do either."

Master Yu said: In the practice of ritual, naturalness is what counts most. This was the beauty of the way of the ancient kings, who let it guide them in matters small and great. Yet it does not hold in every case: to value ease for its own sake, and let it run on without the discipline of ritual, will not do either.

Master Yu said, "When a promise keeps close to what is right, you can make your word good. When respect keeps close to ritual, you stay clear of shame. When the man you lean on is the right man to be close to, you can take him for your guide."

Master Yu said: If your promises are in keeping with what is right, you can make good on what you have said. If your courtesy is in keeping with ritual, you keep clear of shame and disgrace. And if those you depend on are the kind worth being close to, you can take them as your guides.

The Master said, "A gentleman does not ask that his food be rich or his home be easy. He is quick in his work and careful in his speech, and he goes where men of the Way are, to be set straight by them. Call such a man a lover of learning."

The Master said: A cultivated person does not seek to stuff himself at meals or to live in comfort. He is diligent in his work and careful in his speech; he keeps close to those who have the way, and lets them set him straight. Such a person may truly be said to love learning.

Tsze-kung said, "Poor, but no flatterer; rich, but not proud — what would you say to that?" The Master said, "Good. But not so good as poor and glad, or rich and in love with ritual." Tsze-kung said, "The Book of Poetry says, 'Cut, then file; carve, then polish.' Is that what you mean?" The Master said, "Now I can begin to talk about the odes with Ts'ze. Tell him what came before, and he knows what comes next."

Tsze-kung said: Poor, but not fawning; rich, but not arrogant — what would you say of that? The Master said: Good enough; but not so good as poor and yet glad of heart, rich and yet a lover of ritual. Tsze-kung said: The Book of Poetry says, 'As you cut and then file, as you carve and then polish.' Is that not the very thing you mean? The Master said: With Ts'ze I can begin to talk about the odes! Tell him one thing, and he sees what follows from it.
The Master said, "Do not be troubled that men do not know you. Be troubled that you do not know men."
The Master said: I am not troubled that others do not know me; I am troubled that I do not know them.
The Master said, "Govern by virtue, and you are like the north star: it keeps its place, and all the stars turn about it."
The Master said: To govern by virtue is like the north star, which holds its place while all the other stars turn toward it.
The Master said, "The Book of Poetry holds three hundred pieces, and one phrase covers them all: no crooked thoughts."
The Master said: The Book of Poetry has three hundred pieces, but one line covers them all — "Let there be no crooked thoughts."

The Master said, "Lead the people with laws and level them with punishments, and they will dodge the punishment and feel no shame. Lead them with virtue and level them with ritual, and they will feel shame — and set themselves right."

The Master said: Lead the people by laws and keep them in line with punishments, and they will stay out of trouble but feel no shame. Lead them by virtue and keep them in line with ritual, and they will have a sense of shame, and more: they will set themselves right.

The Master said, "At fifteen, I set my heart on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew Heaven's will. At sixty, my ear was tuned to it. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired without crossing the line."

The Master said: At fifteen I set my heart on learning. At thirty I stood firm. At forty I had no more doubts. At fifty I understood the will of Heaven. At sixty my ear was attuned to the truth. At seventy I could follow my heart's desire without overstepping what is right.

Mang I asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Never disobey." Later, as Fan Ch'ih was driving him, the Master said, "Mang-sun asked me about filial devotion, and I told him: never disobey." Fan Ch'ih said, "What did you mean by it?" The Master said, "While they live, serve your parents by ritual. When they die, bury them by ritual, and sacrifice to them by ritual."

Mang I asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Never disobey. Later, when Fan Ch'ih was driving him, the Master said: Mang-sun asked me about filial piety, and I told him — never disobey. Fan Ch'ih asked: What did you mean? The Master said: While parents live, serve them according to ritual; when they die, bury them according to ritual, and make the offerings to them according to ritual.
Mang Wu asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Give your father and mother nothing to worry about except your health."
Mang Wu asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Give your parents no cause for worry but your health.
Tsze-yu asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Nowadays, filial devotion means keeping one's parents fed. But dogs and horses are kept fed too. Without reverence, where is the difference?"
Tsze-yu asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Nowadays "filial" just means feeding your parents. But even dogs and horses get fed. Without reverence, what is the difference?

Tsze-hsia asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "The face is the hard part. When there is work, the young shoulder it; when there is wine and food, the elders are served first — is that all it is to be a devoted son?"

Tsze-hsia asked what filial piety is. The Master said: It is the face that is hard. When there is work to be done, the young take the burden; when there is wine and food, they set it before their elders — but is that all there is to it?

The Master said, "I could talk with Hui all day and he would not once differ with me, as if he were slow. But when he had gone, I watched what he did on his own, and it unfolded everything I had taught him. Hui is not slow."

The Master said: I talked with Hui a whole day, and he never disagreed with anything, like a dullard. But after he left I watched how he lived on his own, and found he could draw out everything I taught. Hui is no dullard.
The Master said, "See what a man does. Look into why he does it. Find where he comes to rest. How can a man stay hidden? How can a man stay hidden?"
The Master said: Watch what a man does. Look into his reasons. See where he comes to rest. How then can a man hide himself? How can a man hide himself?
The Master said, "Keep the old warm and know the new, and you are fit to teach."
The Master said: Keep your old learning warm and gather new — then you are fit to teach others.
The Master said, "A gentleman is not a vessel."
The Master said: A gentleman is not a tool.
Tsze-kung asked about the gentleman. The Master said, "He acts first. Then his words follow his acts."
Tsze-kung asked about the gentleman. The Master said: He acts first, and then speaks according to what he has done.
The Master said, "The gentleman is broad, not partisan. The small man is partisan, not broad."
The Master said: The gentleman draws people together and takes no sides; the small man takes sides and draws no one together.
The Master said, "Learning without thought is labor lost. Thought without learning is dangerous."
The Master said: Learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is dangerous.
The Master said, "To give your strength to strange doctrines — that is harm indeed."
The Master said: To study strange doctrines is harm indeed.
The Master said, "Yu, shall I teach you what it is to know? When you know a thing, hold that you know it. When you do not, admit that you do not. That is knowing."
The Master said: Yu, shall I teach you what knowing is? When you know a thing, to know that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to know that you do not know it — that is knowing.

Tsze-chang was studying with his eye on a salary. The Master said, "Hear much, set aside what is doubtful, and speak carefully about the rest, and you will seldom be blamed. See much, set aside what is dangerous, and act carefully on the rest, and you will seldom be sorry. Words that draw little blame and acts that leave little regret — the salary is in there."

Tsze-chang was studying with an eye to a salaried post. The Master said: Hear much, set aside what you doubt, and speak the rest with care — then you give little cause for blame. See much, set aside what seems risky, and act on the rest with care — then you give little cause for regret. Few occasions for blame in your words, few occasions for regret in your deeds — and the salary will take care of itself.

Duke Ai asked, "What must I do to make the people submit?" Confucius replied, "Raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and the people will submit. Raise the crooked and set them above the straight, and the people will not submit."

Duke Ai asked: What should I do to make the people obey? Confucius answered: Raise up the upright and set them above the crooked, and the people will obey. Raise up the crooked and set them above the upright, and the people will not obey.

Chi K'ang asked how to make the people reverent and loyal, and eager for virtue. The Master said, "Preside over them with gravity, and they will be reverent. Be a devoted son and a kind master, and they will be loyal. Raise up the good and teach the unable, and they will spur one another on."

Chi K'ang asked how to make the people respect their ruler, be loyal to him, and spur one another to virtue. The Master said: Face them with dignity, and they will respect you. Be devoted to your own parents and kind to all, and they will be loyal. Promote the able and teach those who fall short, and they will spur one another on.

Someone said to Confucius, "Sir, why do you take no part in government?" The Master said, "The Shu-ching says of filial devotion: 'Be devoted to your parents and a friend to your brothers, and it will carry into government.' That too is governing. Why must a man hold office to govern?"

Someone asked Confucius: Sir, why are you not in government? The Master said: The Book of History says of filial piety — "Be filial, simply be filial, and a good brother, and you carry this over into government." That too is to take part in government. Why must one hold office to be in government?
The Master said, "A man whose word cannot be trusted — I do not know what he is good for. A big cart without a yoke-bar, a small cart without a collar-pin: how do you make them go?"
The Master said: I do not see how a man without good faith can get along. How can a wagon move without the yoke-bar for the oxen, or a carriage without the cross-pin for the horses?

Tsze-chang asked whether what comes ten generations from now can be known. Confucius said, "The Yin took its rites from the Hsia; what it dropped and what it added can be known. The Chau took its rites from the Yin; what it dropped and what it added can be known. And whoever follows the Chau — though a hundred generations pass, it can be known."

Tsze-chang asked whether the next ten generations could be known. Confucius said: The Yin took over the rituals of the Hsia, and what they dropped or added can be known. The Chau took over the rituals of the Yin, and what they dropped or added can be known. Whoever comes after the Chau, even a hundred generations on, can be known in the same way.
The Master said, "To sacrifice to a spirit that is not your own is flattery. To see what is right and not do it is cowardice."
The Master said: To sacrifice to a spirit that is not your own is mere flattery. To see what is right and fail to do it is cowardice.
Confucius said of the head of the Chi family, who had eight rows of dancers perform in his courtyard, "If he can bear to do this, what can he not bear to do?"
Of the head of the Chi family, who had eight rows of dancers performing in his courtyard, the Master said: If he can stomach this, what can he not stomach?

The three families had the Yung ode sung while the sacrificial vessels were cleared. The Master said, "'The princes assist; the son of heaven, deep and grave.' What can those words mean in the hall of the three families?"

The three families had the Yung ode sung as the vessels were cleared away at the end of their sacrifice. The Master said: "Assisting are the princes; the son of Heaven looks deep and grave" — what business have those words in the hall of three private families?
The Master said, "A man without human-heartedness — what is ritual to him? A man without human-heartedness — what is music to him?"
The Master said: A man without humaneness — what has he to do with ritual? A man without humaneness — what has he to do with music?
Lin Fang asked what comes first in ritual. The Master said, "A great question! In festival, better spare than lavish. In mourning, better grief than a flawless performance."
Lin Fang asked what matters most in ceremony. The Master said: A great question indeed! In ceremony, better plain than lavish. In mourning, better real grief than smooth observance.
The Master said, "The tribes of the east and north still have their princes. They are not like our great land, which goes without."
The Master said: The rude tribes of the east and north still have their rulers — unlike the states of our own great land, who have lost theirs.

The head of the Chi family was about to sacrifice to the T'ai mountain. The Master said to Zan Yu, "Can you not save him from this?" He answered, "I cannot." The Master said, "Alas! Will you tell me the T'ai mountain is less discerning than Lin Fang?"

The head of the Chi family was about to sacrifice to Mount T'ai. The Master said to Zan Yu: Can you not stop him? Zan Yu said: I cannot. The Master said: Alas! Will you tell me that Mount T'ai knows less of ritual than Lin Fang?

The Master said, "A gentleman has nothing to contend for. If contend he must, let it be at archery: he bows to his rivals and goes up, comes down again and drinks the forfeit. Even in his contending, he is a gentleman."

The Master said: The cultivated person has nothing to compete over. If you must find him competing, let it be at archery — yet even there he bows to his rivals as he goes up, bows again as he comes down, and drinks the loser's cup. Even in contest he stays a cultivated person.

Tsze-hsia asked, "What do these lines mean — 'The dimples of her artful smile, the clear black and white of her eye, the plain ground for the colors'?" The Master said, "The colors come after the plain ground." "Then ritual comes after?" The Master said, "It is Shang who lifts my meaning. Now I can begin to talk about the odes with him."

Tsze-hsia asked: What does this mean — "Her dimpled smile so winning, her dark eyes so clear; the plain ground waits for the colors"? The Master said: The colors go on after the plain ground is laid. Tsze-hsia said: Then ritual comes after? The Master said: It is Shang who draws out my meaning. Now I can begin to talk about the odes with him.

The Master said, "I could describe the rites of the Hsia, but Chi cannot bear witness for me. I could describe the rites of the Yin, but Sung cannot bear witness for me. Their records and their wise men are too few. Were they enough, I could call on them to prove my words."

The Master said: I can describe the rituals of the Hsia, but the state of Chi cannot bear me out. I can describe the rituals of the Yin, but the state of Sung cannot bear me out — their records and their wise men have run too thin. Were they enough, I could prove every word.
The Master said, "At the great sacrifice, once the opening libation is poured, I have no wish to watch what follows."
The Master said: At the great sacrifice, once the first libation has been poured, I have no wish to watch the rest.
Someone asked the meaning of the great sacrifice. The Master said, "I do not know. To the man who knew, the whole kingdom would lie as plain as this" — and he pointed to his palm.
Someone asked the meaning of the great sacrifice. The Master said: I do not know. To one who knew, governing the world would be as easy as this — and he pointed to his palm.

He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present. He sacrificed to the spirits as if the spirits were there. The Master said, "If I am not present at the sacrifice myself, it is as if I had not sacrificed."

He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present; he sacrificed to the spirits as if the spirits were present. The Master said: If I am not there myself at the sacrifice, it is as though I had not sacrificed at all.
Wang-sun Chia asked, "What does the saying mean — 'Better to court the kitchen stove than the southwest corner'?" The Master said, "Not so. A man who sins against Heaven has no one left to pray to."

Wang-sun Chia asked: What does the saying mean — "Better to court the kitchen stove than the honored corner of the room"? The Master said: Not so. Offend against Heaven, and there is no one left to pray to.
The Master said, "Chau had two dynasties to look back on. How full, how fine its pattern! I follow Chau."
The Master said: Chau could look back on the two dynasties before it. How rich and refined its forms are! I follow Chau.

The Master, entering the grand temple, asked about everything. Someone said, "Who calls the son of the man of Tsau a master of ritual? He enters the grand temple and asks about everything." The Master heard of it and said, "The asking is the ritual."

When the Master entered the grand temple, he asked about everything. Someone said: Who claimed that the son of the man of Tsau knows ritual? He enters the grand temple and asks about everything. When the Master heard it, he said: That itself is ritual.
The Master said, "In archery, piercing the hide is not the point, for men's strength is not equal. That was the old way."
The Master said: In archery, piercing the hide is not the point — for men differ in strength. So it was in the old way.
Tsze-kung wanted to do away with the sheep offered at the announcing of each new moon. The Master said, "Ts'ze, you love the sheep. I love the rite."
Tsze-kung wanted to do away with the sheep offered at the start of each new month. The Master said: Ts'ze, you grudge the sheep; I care for the ritual.
The Master said, "Serve your prince with the whole of ritual, and men will call it flattery."
The Master said: Serve your ruler with the full measure of ritual, and people will call it flattery.

Duke Ting asked how a prince should use his ministers, and how ministers should serve their prince. Confucius replied, "The prince uses his ministers according to ritual. The ministers serve their prince with loyalty."

Duke Ting asked how a ruler should use his ministers, and how ministers should serve their ruler. Confucius answered: A ruler should use his ministers according to ritual; ministers should serve their ruler with faithfulness.
The Master said, "The Kwan Tsu: joy, but never license; grief, but never a wound."
The Master said: The Kwan Tsu ode is joyful without going wanton, and sorrowful without breaking into grief.

Duke Ai asked Tsai Wo about the altars of the land. Tsai Wo replied, "The sovereigns of Hsia planted them with pine; the men of Yin, with cypress; the men of Chau, with chestnut — to make the people tremble, they said." When the Master heard of it, he said, "What is done, do not discuss. What has run its course, do not contest. What is past, do not blame."

Duke Ai asked Tsai Wo about the altars to the spirits of the land. Tsai Wo said: The Hsia kings planted pine around them, the men of Yin planted cypress, and the men of Chau planted chestnut — chestnut, they said, to make the people tremble. When the Master heard it, he said: What is done, do not preach about; what has run its course, do not push against; what is past, do not blame.

The Master said, "Kwan Chung was a small vessel!" Someone said, "Was Kwan Chung frugal, then?" "Kwan had the San Kwei, and no officer of his did double duty. How is that frugal?" "Then did Kwan Chung know ritual?" The Master said, "The princes of states set a screen before their gates; Kwan set a screen before his too. When two princes met in friendship, they had a stand for the turned-down cups; Kwan had such a stand too. If Kwan knew ritual, who does not know ritual?"

The Master said: How small a vessel was Kwan Chung! Someone said: Was Kwan Chung frugal, then? The Master said: Kwan kept three separate establishments, and none of his officers held a second post — how can you call him frugal? Then did Kwan Chung at least know ritual? The Master said: The ruler of a state screens his gate; Kwan too screened his gate. When two rulers meet in friendship, they have a stand for the inverted cups; Kwan too had such a stand. If Kwan Chung knew ritual, then who does not?

The Master, instructing the grand music-master of Lu, said, "This much of music can be known. It opens with all the parts sounding together. Then, given rein, they run pure and clear, each voice distinct, unbroken — and so to the close."

The Master said to the grand music-master of Lu: Music can be understood. It begins with all the parts sounding as one; as it unfolds they move in harmony, each clear and distinct, flowing on unbroken — and so to the close.

The border warden at Yi asked to be presented to the Master. "When men of worth have come to this place," he said, "I have never been refused." The followers presented him, and when he came out he said, "Friends, why grieve over your master's fall from office? The world has long been without the Way. Heaven is going to use your master as a bell with a wooden tongue."

The border warden at Yi asked to be presented to the Master, saying: When men of worth have passed this way, I have never been refused the meeting. The followers brought him in, and when he came out he said: My friends, why be troubled that your master has lost his post? The world has long been without the way; Heaven is about to make of your master a bell to rouse it.
The Master said of the Shao music that it was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good, and of the Wu that it was perfectly beautiful, but not perfectly good.
The Master said of the Shao music that it was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good. Of the Wu music he said it was perfectly beautiful but not perfectly good.
The Master said, "High place without largeness of spirit, ritual without reverence, mourning without grief — what is there for me to look at?"
The Master said: High place held without generosity; ritual performed without reverence; mourning gone through without grief — how could I bear to look on such things?
The Master said, "It is human-heartedness that makes a neighborhood beautiful. If a man can choose where to live and passes it by, how is he wise?"
The Master said: It is the humaneness of a neighborhood that makes it good. If a man, in choosing where to settle, does not settle among the humane, how can he be called wise?
The Master said, "Without human-heartedness, a man cannot bear hardship long, and he cannot bear comfort long either. The human-hearted rest in it. The wise know what it is worth."
The Master said: Those without humaneness cannot rest for long in hardship, nor for long in ease. The humane are at home in their humaneness; the wise turn it to good use.
The Master said, "Only the human-hearted man can rightly love men, and rightly hate them."
The Master said: Only the humane man knows how to love others, and how to hate them.
The Master said, "Set your will on human-heartedness, and there is no room left for evil."
The Master said: Once the will is set on humaneness, there is no room left for doing wrong.

The Master said, "Riches and rank are what men want; if they cannot be had in the right way, do not hold them. Poverty and low place are what men hate; if they cannot be escaped in the right way, do not escape them. Take human-heartedness from a gentleman, and what is left of the name? A gentleman does not leave it for the length of a meal. In a hurry, he holds to it. In danger, he holds to it."

The Master said: Wealth and rank are what men desire; but if they cannot be had in the right way, do not hold on to them. Poverty and obscurity are what men dislike; but if they cannot be escaped in the right way, do not escape them. If a cultivated person abandons humaneness, how can he live up to the name? The cultivated person does not part from humaneness for the space of a single meal. In moments of haste he holds fast to it; in times of danger he holds fast to it.

The Master said, "I have never seen a man who loved human-heartedness, or one who hated its opposite. The lover would set nothing above it. The hater would practice it by letting nothing opposed to it come near him. Is there a man who can give his strength to it for one day? I have never seen one whose strength was too little. If such a man exists, I have not seen him."

The Master said: I have never seen a man who truly loved humaneness, nor one who truly hated what is inhumane. A man who loved humaneness would prize nothing above it. A man who hated what is inhumane would so practice humaneness that nothing inhumane could come near him. Is anyone able, for a single day, to put all his strength into humaneness? I have never seen a man whose strength was not enough. There may be such a case — but I have never seen it.
The Master said, "A man's faults run true to his kind. Look at the faults, and you know the human-heartedness."
The Master said: A man's faults belong to his kind. Look closely at a man's faults, and you will know whether he is humane.
The Master said, "Hear the Way in the morning, and you can die that evening without regret."
The Master said: If in the morning a man hears the Way, in the evening he may die content.
The Master said, "A scholar sets his heart on the Way. If he is ashamed of shabby clothes and plain food, he is not worth talking to."
The Master said: A man of learning whose heart is set on the Way, yet who is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food, is not worth talking to.
The Master said, "The gentleman moves through the world with nothing fixed for and nothing fixed against. He goes with what is right."
The Master said: In his dealings with the world, the cultivated person is neither for anything nor against anything; he sides with what is right.
The Master said, "The gentleman thinks of virtue; the small man thinks of comfort. The gentleman thinks of what the law will exact; the small man thinks of what favor he can win."
The Master said: The cultivated person thinks of virtue; the small man thinks of comfort. The cultivated person thinks of the law; the small man thinks of favors.
The Master said, "Act always with an eye to your own advantage, and you will be much resented."
The Master said: A man who acts always with an eye to his own gain will stir up much resentment.
The Master said, "If a man can govern his country by ritual and its deference, what difficulty will he have? And if he cannot, what is ritual to him?"
The Master said: If a ruler can govern with the courtesy that ritual asks for, what difficulty will he have? If he cannot govern with that courtesy, what has he to do with ritual at all?
The Master said, "Do not worry that you have no position; worry about what it takes to stand in one. Do not worry that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing."
The Master said: Do not be troubled that you have no position; be troubled that you are not fit for one. Do not be troubled that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing.

The Master said, "Shan, one thread runs through my Way." Master Tsang said, "Yes." The Master went out, and the other disciples asked, "What did he mean?" Master Tsang said, "The Master's Way is loyalty, and putting yourself in the other man's place. That is all."

The Master said: Shan, my Way is threaded on a single thread. Master Tsang said: Yes. When the Master had gone out, the other disciples asked: What did he mean? Master Tsang said: The Way of the Master is just this — wholeheartedness toward others, and weighing their hearts as your own. That, and nothing more.
The Master said, "The gentleman is at home in what is right; the small man is at home in what pays."
The Master said: The cultivated person understands what is right; the small man understands what is profitable.
The Master said, "When you see a worthy man, think how to equal him. When you see an unworthy one, turn and examine yourself."
The Master said: When you see a worthy person, think of equaling him; when you see an unworthy one, turn inward and examine yourself.

The Master said, "In serving your parents, you may reason with them — gently. If you see they will not follow, be more reverent still, and do not turn back. And though it wears you out, do not resent them."

The Master said: In serving his parents, a son may remonstrate with them, but gently. If he sees they are not inclined to follow him, he is all the more respectful and does not cross them, and though it wears him out, he does not complain.
The Master said, "While your parents live, do not travel far. If travel you must, have a fixed place to go."
The Master said: While his parents are alive, a son should not travel far; and if he does go, he must have a fixed destination.
The Master said, "If for three years a son does not turn from his father's way, he may be called a devoted son."
The Master said: If for three years a son does not depart from his father's ways, he may be called a devoted son.
The Master said, "Your parents' years must never be out of mind — at once a joy and a fear."
The Master said: A son must always keep his parents' age in mind — on the one hand for joy, on the other for fear.
The Master said, "The ancients were slow to speak. They were ashamed to have their deeds fall short of their words."
The Master said: The reason the ancients were slow to speak was that they were ashamed to let their deeds fall short of their words.
The Master said, "Few go wrong by holding back."
The Master said: Those who hold themselves in check rarely go wrong.
The Master said, "The gentleman wants to be slow in his words and quick in his deeds."
The Master said: The cultivated person wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action.
The Master said, "Virtue does not stand alone. It always finds neighbors."
The Master said: Virtue is never left to stand alone. A man who has it will have neighbors.
Tsze-yu said, "Press your prince too often, and you will be disgraced. Press your friends too often, and they will fall away."
Tsze-yu said: Pester a ruler too often, and you bring disgrace on yourself. Reprove a friend too often, and you drive him away.
The Master said of Kung-ye Ch'ang that he was fit to be given a wife: he had been in bonds, but the guilt was never his. And he gave him his own daughter in marriage.

The Master said of Kung-ye Ch'ang that he was fit to marry: though he had once been put in chains, it was through no crime of his own. And he gave him his own daughter in marriage. Of Nan Yung he said that in a well-governed state he would not be passed over for office, and in a badly governed one he would keep clear of punishment and disgrace. And he gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.

Of Nan Yung the Master said that in a well-governed country he would never be out of office, and in an ill-governed one he would keep clear of punishment and disgrace. He gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
The Master said of Tsze-chien: A man of fine character, this one! Yet if Lu had no men of worth, where would he have gotten it?
The Master said of Tsze-chien, "There is a gentleman! If Lu held no gentlemen, where did this man get it?"
Tsze-kung asked: And what do you make of me? The Master said: You are a vessel. What vessel? A jeweled vessel for the sacrifice.
Tsze-kung asked, "And Ts'ze — what do you say of him?" The Master said, "You are a vessel." "What kind of vessel?" "A jeweled vessel for the altar."

Someone said: Yung is humane, but he has no gift for talk. The Master said: What is the good of a gift for talk? Meet people with a quick tongue and you mostly earn their dislike. Whether he is humane I do not know — but what does he want with a quick tongue?

Someone said, "Yung is human-hearted, but he has no ready tongue." The Master said, "What is a ready tongue for? Meet men with a quick mouth and they will hate you for it, more often than not. Whether Yung is human-hearted I do not know — but why should he need a ready tongue?"
The Master was urging Ch'i-tiao K'ai to take office. He answered: I cannot yet feel sure of myself in this. The Master was pleased.
The Master wanted Ch'i-tiao K'ai to take office. He replied, "I cannot yet trust myself so far." The Master was pleased.

The Master said: My way makes no headway. I will get on a raft and put out to sea. The one who would come with me — that would be Yu, I think. Tsze-lu, hearing this, was delighted. The Master said: Yu loves daring more than I do, but he has nowhere to find his timber.

The Master said, "The Way makes no headway. I will board a raft and drift out to sea — and the one who follows me will be Yu, I expect." Tsze-lu, hearing it, was glad. The Master said, "Yu loves daring more than I do. But he does not stop to weigh the thing."

Mang Wu asked whether Tsze-lu was humane. The Master said: I do not know. He asked again. The Master said: In a state of a thousand chariots, Yu could be put in charge of the military levies — but whether he is humane I do not know. And Ch'iu? The Master said: In a town of a thousand households, or a clan of a hundred chariots, Ch'iu could be made its governor — but whether he is humane I do not know. And Ch'ih? The Master said: Standing in his sash at court, Ch'ih could be set to deal with the guests and envoys — but whether he is humane I do not know.

Mang Wu asked whether Tsze-lu was human-hearted. The Master said, "I do not know." He asked again, and the Master said, "In a state of a thousand chariots, Yu could be given the levies to manage. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know." "And what of Ch'iu?" The Master said, "In a town of a thousand households, or a house of a hundred chariots, Ch'iu could be made steward. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know." "And what of Ch'ih?" The Master said, "With his sash bound, standing in court, Ch'ih could be set to talk with the guests and visitors. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know."

The Master said to Tsze-kung: Which is the better, you or Hui? He answered: How could I dare compare myself with Hui? Hui hears one thing and understands ten; I hear one thing and understand two. The Master said: You are not his equal. I grant you — you and I are both not his equal.

The Master said to Tsze-kung, "Which of you is the better, you or Hui?" Tsze-kung replied, "How could I dare look as high as Hui? Hui hears one thing and knows ten. I hear one thing and know two." The Master said, "No, you are not his equal. You and I — neither of us is his equal."

Tsai Yu was asleep in the daytime. The Master said: Rotten wood cannot be carved, a wall of dung cannot be plastered. With Yu — what is the use of reproaching him? The Master said: There was a time when I heard a man's words and trusted his conduct; now I hear his words and watch his conduct. It is Yu who has made me change.

Tsai Yu lay asleep in the daytime. The Master said, "Rotten wood cannot be carved. A wall of dung and mud takes no trowel. Why should I even scold Yu?" The Master said, "There was a time when I heard a man's words and trusted his deeds to match. Now I hear the words and watch the deeds. Yu changed that in me."
The Master said: I have never seen a man truly unbending. Someone said: There is Shan Ch'ang. The Master said: Ch'ang is ruled by his cravings — how can he be unbending?
The Master said, "I have never seen a man who is truly unbending." Someone answered, "Shan Ch'ang." The Master said, "Ch'ang? Ch'ang is full of desires. Where would he get unbending?"
Tsze-kung said: What I do not want others to do to me, I also want not to do to others. The Master said: Ts'ze, that is beyond you yet.
Tsze-kung said, "What I do not want done to me, I want to do to no one." The Master said, "Ts'ze, that is beyond you."
Tsze-kung said: One can hear the Master on questions of culture and conduct. One cannot hear him on the nature of man or the way of Heaven.
Tsze-kung said, "The Master's culture and conduct — these we are given to hear. What the Master says of our nature and of the Way of Heaven, no one gets to hear."
When Tsze-lu had heard something and had not yet been able to act on it, his one fear was that he might hear something more.
When Tsze-lu had heard a thing and not yet carried it out, his one fear was hearing another.
Tsze-kung asked: Why was Kung-wan given the title "Cultured"? The Master said: He was quick and a lover of learning, and not ashamed to ask of those beneath him. That is why he was called "Cultured."

Tsze-kung asked, "Why was Kung-wan given the name Wan — 'the cultured'?" The Master said, "He was quick, and he loved learning, and he was not ashamed to ask those beneath him. That is why they called him Wan."

The Master said of Tsze-ch'an that he had four marks of the cultivated man: in his own bearing he was humble; in serving those above him, respectful; in providing for the people, kind; in directing the people, just.

The Master said of Tsze-ch'an that he had four marks of the gentleman: in his own conduct he was humble; in serving his superiors, respectful; in providing for the people, kind; in commanding them, just.
The Master said: Yen P'ing knew how to keep a friendship. However long he had known a man, he showed him the same respect as at first.
The Master said, "Yen P'ing knew how to keep a friend. However long he knew a man, his respect was what it had been on the first day."
The Master said: Tsang Wan housed his great tortoise in a hall with mountains carved on the pillar-tops and waterweed painted on the beams. What sort of wisdom was that?
The Master said, "Tsang Wan housed a great tortoise in a hall of its own, with hills carved on the pillar-tops and duckweed painted on the posts above the beams. What kind of wisdom is that?"

Tsze-chang asked: The minister Tsze-wan took office three times and showed no joy, and three times was dismissed and showed no resentment; each time he handed the old government over fully to his successor. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was loyal. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane? Tsze-chang went on: When Ts'ui killed the prince of Ch'i, Ch'an Wan, who owned forty horses, abandoned them and left the country. Coming to another state, he said, "They are no better here than our own officer Ts'ui," and left. He came to a second state, said the same, and left again. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was clean. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane?

Tsze-chang asked, "The minister Tsze-wan took office three times and showed no pleasure, and was removed three times and showed no resentment — and each time he gave the incoming minister a full account of his government. What do you say of him?" The Master said, "He was loyal." "Was he human-hearted?" "I do not know. Where is the human-heartedness in it?" Tsze-chang went on, "When the officer Ch'ui killed the prince of Ch'i, Ch'an Wan, who owned forty horses, abandoned them and left the country. In the next state, he said, 'They are like our officer Ch'ui here,' and left. He came to a third, said the same, and left again. What do you say of him?" The Master said, "He was clean." "Was he human-hearted?" "I do not know. Where is the human-heartedness in it?"
Chi Wan thought three times before he acted. The Master, hearing of it, said: Twice is enough.
Chi Wan thought three times before he acted. When the Master heard of it, he said, "Twice is enough."
The Master said: When the country was well governed, Ning Wu played the wise man; when it fell into disorder, he played the fool. His wisdom others may match — his folly they cannot.
The Master said, "While the country kept the Way, Ning Wu was wise. When the country lost it, he played the fool. His wisdom can be matched. His folly cannot."

When the Master was in Ch'an he said: Let me go home! Let me go home! The young ones of my school are headstrong and rash; they have made a fine, finished start, but do not know how to cut and shape themselves.
When the Master was in Ch'an, he said, "Home — let me go home! The young men of my school are bold and hasty. They weave brilliant cloth, and they do not know how to cut it."
The Master said: Po-i and Shu-ch'i held no man's old wrongs against him, and so they were little resented.
The Master said, "Po-i and Shu-ch'i did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so the grudges against them were few."
The Master said: Who calls Wei-shang Kao straight? A man begged vinegar of him, and he begged it from a neighbor and gave it as his own.
The Master said, "Who calls Wei-shang Kao upright? A man begged vinegar of him, and he begged it from his neighbor and gave it as his own."

The Master said: Smooth words, a fawning look, and overdone respect — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of them, and so am I. To hide a grudge against a man and act the friend to him — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of that, and so am I.

The Master said, "Clever words, a winning face, respect laid on thick — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of them, and so am I. To hide a grudge against a man and treat him as a friend — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of that, and so am I."

Yen Yuan and Chi Lu were at his side. The Master said: Why not each of you tell me what you long for? Tsze-lu said: I would have my carriage and horses and fine fur coats to share with my friends, and not mind if they wore them out. Yen Yuan said: I would not boast of my goodness or make a show of my labors. Tsze-lu said: And now we would hear the Master's longing. The Master said: To give the old their rest, to give friends my trust, and to cherish the young.

Yen Yuan and Chi Lu were at his side. The Master said, "Come, why not each of you tell me his wish?" Tsze-lu said, "I would share my chariots and horses and light furs with my friends, and if they wore them to ruin, think nothing of it." Yen Yuan said, "I would never boast of what is good in me, nor parade what I have done." Tsze-lu said, "And now, sir, we would hear your wish." The Master said, "To give the old rest. To keep faith with friends. To cherish the young."
The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to meet the man who can see his own faults and arraign himself within.
The Master said, "It is hopeless. I have yet to see a man who could look at his own faults and press the case against himself."
The Master said, "In a hamlet of ten houses there is surely someone as loyal and true as I am. But no one who loves learning as I do."
The Master said: In a hamlet of ten households there is sure to be someone as loyal and true as I am — but none so fond of learning.

sections.label: Book VI
sections.title: Knowing, Loving, Delighting
On Disciples and the Humane Life

segments.text: The Master said, “Yung — you could seat him on a throne.” Chung-kung asked about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. The Master said, “He will do. He keeps things simple.” Chung-kung said, “If a man is exacting with himself and simple in what he asks of his people, that is fine. But to be easy on yourself and easy in everything you do — isn’t that carrying simplicity too far?” The Master said, “Yung is right.”

The Master said: There is Yung — he could be seated facing south, like a prince. Chung-kung asked about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. The Master said: He will do; he does not fuss over small matters. Chung-kung said: To hold reverence within yourself and yet keep an easy hand in small matters when you govern the people — that may pass. But to be easy within and easy without as well — is that not too easy by far? The Master said: Yung is right.

The Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved to learn. Confucius answered, “There was Yen Hui. He loved to learn. He never took his anger out on the wrong man; he never made the same mistake twice. But his time was short, and he died. Now there is no one — I have yet to hear of anyone who loves learning the way he did.”

Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved learning. Confucius answered: There was Yen Hui; he loved to learn. He never turned his anger on the wrong person, and he never made the same mistake twice. Sadly, his life was cut short and he died; and now there is no one like him. I have not heard of anyone since who loves learning as he did.

When Tsze-hwa was sent on a mission to Ch’i, the disciple Zan asked for grain for Tsze-hwa’s mother. The Master said, “Give her a fu.” Zan asked for more. “Give her a yu,” said the Master. Zan gave her five ping. The Master said, “When Ch’ih set out for Ch’i, he rode behind sleek horses in light furs. And I have always heard: a gentleman helps the desperate; he does not top up the rich.” When the Master made Yuan Sze governor of his town, he gave him nine hundred measures of grain. Sze declined them. The Master said, “Don’t. Could you not give it away — to your neighborhood, your hamlet, your village?”

When Tsze-hwa was sent on a mission to Ch'i, the disciple Zan asked for grain to provide for Tsze-hwa's mother. The Master said: Give her a fu. Zan asked for more. Give her an yu, said the Master. Zan gave her five ping. The Master said: When Ch'ih set out for Ch'i, he had sleek horses to his carriage and wore fine furs. I have heard that the cultivated person relieves the hard-pressed, but does not add to the riches of the rich.
The Master said of Chung-kung, “If the calf of a brindled ox is red and well-horned, men may hesitate to offer it — but will the spirits of the mountains and rivers refuse it?”

When Yuan Sze was made governor of his town, the Master granted him nine hundred measures of grain, and Sze declined them. The Master said: Do not refuse. Could you not pass them on to the neighborhoods, the hamlets, and the villages around you?
The Master said, “Hui could go three months without his heart once straying from human-heartedness. The others manage a day here, a month there, and no more.”

Speaking of Chung-kung, the Master said: If the calf of a plowing ox is red-coated and well-horned, then even if men would rather not offer it, will the spirits of the mountains and rivers turn it away?

Chi K’ang asked whether Chung-yu was fit for office. The Master said, “Yu is decisive. What trouble would office give him?” “And Ts’ze — is he fit for office?” “Ts’ze sees through things. What trouble would office give him?” “And Ch’iu?” “Ch’iu has many talents. What trouble would office give him?”
The Master said: Such was Hui — for three months together his heart would not stray from humaneness. The others may reach it for a day or a month, and no more.
The head of the Chi family sent for Min Tsze-ch’ien to be governor of Pi. Min Tsze-ch’ien said, “Decline for me — politely. If anyone comes back a second time, they will find me across the Wan.”

Chi K'ang asked whether Chung-yu was fit to hold office. The Master said: Yu is decisive; what trouble would he have holding office? And is Ts'ze fit to hold office? The Master said: Ts'ze sees into things; what trouble would he have holding office? And Ch'iu? The Master said: Ch'iu has many talents; what trouble would he have holding office?

Po-niu was sick, and the Master went to see him. Taking his hand through the window, he said, “We are losing him. It is Heaven’s decree — and yet, that this man should have this disease! That this man should have this disease!”

The head of the Chi family sent to make Min Tsze-ch'ien governor of Pi. Min Tsze-ch'ien said: Make my excuses for me, gently. If anyone comes asking a second time, I shall have to cross the Wan and leave the country.
The Master said, “What a man Hui was! One bowl of rice, one gourd of water, a hovel in a back lane — no one else could have borne the misery, and it never once touched his joy. What a man Hui was!”

When Po-niu was ill, the Master went to ask after him. He took his hand through the window and said: He is lost — it is the will of Heaven, alas. That such a man should have such a sickness! That such a man should have such a sickness!

Yen Ch’iu said, “It is not that I take no delight in your Way, Master. I lack the strength.” The Master said, “Those who lack the strength give out somewhere along the road. You have drawn your line before setting out.”

The Master said: What a fine character Hui had! A bowl of rice, a gourd of water, a poor man's lane to live in — others could not have borne such misery, yet it never spoiled Hui's joy. What a fine character Hui had!
The Master said to Tsze-hsia, “Be a scholar of the gentleman’s kind, not the small man’s.”

Yen Ch'iu said: It is not that I take no delight in your Way; my strength is not enough for it. The Master said: Those whose strength is not enough give out halfway along the road. You are drawing your own line before you start.

When Tsze-yu was governor of Wu-ch’ang, the Master said, “Have you found any good men?” He answered, “There is Tan-t’ai Mieh-ming. He never takes a shortcut, and he has never once come to my office except on public business.”
The Master said to Tsze-hsia: Be a scholar in the manner of the cultivated person, not in the manner of the small man.

The Master said, “Mang Chih-fan does not boast. When the army broke and ran, he kept the rear; only as they reached the gate did he whip up his horse, saying, ‘It was not courage that kept me back. My horse would not go.’”

When Tsze-yu was governor of Wu-ch'ang, the Master asked: Have you found any good men there? He answered: There is Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming. He never takes a shortcut when he walks, and he never comes to my office except on public business.
The Master said, “Without the glib tongue of the litanist T’o or the good looks of prince Chao of Sung, it is hard to get through in the present age.”

The Master said: Mang Chih-fan never boasts of what he does. When the army was in flight he brought up the rear, and as they reached the gate he whipped his horse forward and said: It was not that I dared to come last — my horse would not go any faster.
The Master said, “Who leaves a house except by the door? Why, then, will no one walk by this Way?”
The Master said: Without the smooth tongue of the priest T'o and the good looks of Prince Chao of Sung, it is hard to get through these times unscathed.
The Master said, “When substance outweighs polish, you get a rustic. When polish outweighs substance, you get a clerk. Polish and substance in balance — that is a gentleman.”
The Master said: Who can go out except by the door? Why, then, will no one walk by this Way?
The Master said, “A man is born straight. If he loses that and lives on, he is simply lucky to have escaped.”

The Master said: Where the raw stuff outweighs the polish, a man is coarse; where the polish outweighs the raw stuff, he is a mere clerk. Raw stuff and polish in even measure — there you have the cultivated person.
The Master said, “Those who know it are not the equal of those who love it, and those who love it are not the equal of those who delight in it.”
The Master said: A man is born for uprightness. If a man loses it and lives on, he has only luck to thank that he is not dead.
The Master said, “To those above the average, you may speak of the highest things. To those below it, you may not.”
The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.

Fan Ch’ih asked about wisdom. The Master said, “Give yourself to what is owed to men; respect the spirits, but keep your distance from them. Call that wisdom.” He asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, “The human-hearted man puts the hard work first and any reward out of mind. Call that human-heartedness.”
The Master said: To those above the common run you may speak of the highest things; to those below it you may not.
The Master said, “The wise delight in water; the human-hearted delight in mountains. The wise move; the human-hearted are still. The wise are joyful; the human-hearted live long.”

Fan Ch'ih asked what wisdom is. The Master said: To give yourself wholly to the duties owed to other people, and to honor the spirits while keeping your distance from them — that may be called wisdom. He asked about humaneness. The Master said: The humane person takes on the hard part first and lets the reward come after — that may be called humaneness.
The Master said, “One change, and Ch’i would stand where Lu stands. One change, and Lu would reach the Way.”
The Master said: The wise delight in water; the humane delight in mountains. The wise are active; the humane are still. The wise find joy; the humane find length of days.
The Master said, “A cornered cup with no corners — call that a cornered cup? Call that a cornered cup?”
The Master said: Ch'i, with one change, would rise to the level of Lu; and Lu, with one change, would rise to the level of the Way.

Tsai Wo asked, “Tell a human-hearted man there is a man down the well, and I suppose he jumps in after him?” Confucius said, “Why would he? A gentleman can be sent to the well, but not down it. He can be deceived; he cannot be made a fool of.”
The Master said: A drinking-cup that is no longer a cup — what a cup! What a cup!
The Master said, “A gentleman who studies widely and reins himself in with ritual is not likely to go far wrong.”

Tsai Wo asked: Suppose a humane man were told there was someone down a well — would he go in after him? The Master said: Why would he do that? You may send the cultivated person to the well, but you cannot make him jump in; you may deceive him, but you cannot make a fool of him.
The Master went to see Nan-tsze, and Tsze-lu was not pleased. The Master swore to him, “If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven throw me aside! May Heaven throw me aside!”
The Master said: The cultivated person studies widely in all learning, and reins himself in with ritual; so he too can keep from overstepping what is right.
The Master said, “The virtue of the Constant Mean — how complete it is! And how long it has been rare among the people!”
When the Master had been to see Nan-tsze, Tsze-lu was displeased. The Master swore an oath: If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven cast me off! May Heaven cast me off!

Tsze-kung said, “What about a man who poured out benefits on the people and could help them all — what would you say? Could he be called human-hearted?” The Master said, “Why stop at human-hearted? He would be a sage. Even Yao and Shun fell short of that. The human-hearted man is this: wanting to stand, he helps others to stand; wanting to arrive, he helps others arrive. To take what is near — yourself — as the measure for others: that is the way to human-heartedness.”
The Master said: The virtue of the Constant Mean — how perfect it is! And how long it has been rare among the people.

Tsze-kung said: Suppose a man who showered benefits on the people and could bring help to all — what would you say of him? Could he be called humane? The Master said: Why stop at humane? Surely he would be a sage. Even Yao and Shun fell short of that. As for the humane person: wishing to stand on his own feet, he helps others to stand; wishing to reach his goal, he helps others to reach theirs. To take what is near at hand — yourself — as the measure of others: that may be called the practice of humaneness.
The Master said, “I transmit; I do not invent. I trust the ancients and I love them. Quietly, I compare myself to our old P’ang.”
The Master said: A transmitter and not a maker, trusting and loving the ancients — in this I venture to liken myself to our old P'ang.
The Master said, “To store up knowledge in silence, to learn without tiring, to teach without wearing out — which of these can I claim?”
The Master said: To store up knowledge in silence, to learn without ever tiring, to teach others without growing weary — which of these have I mastered?
The Master said, “Virtue left untended; learning left undiscussed; hearing what is right and failing to move toward it; being unable to change what is bad in me — these are the things that worry me.”

The Master said: That I leave my character untended, that I fail to dig deep into what I learn, that I hear what is right and cannot move toward it, that I see my faults and cannot mend them — these are the things that trouble me.
In his leisure hours the Master was easy and unbent, his face open and pleased.
When the Master was at his ease, his manner was relaxed and his face content.
The Master said, “How far I have sunk! How long it has been since I dreamed of the duke of Chau.”
The Master said: How far I have declined! It is a long time now since I dreamed, as I used to, of the duke of Chau.
The Master said, “Set your heart on the Way. Hold fast to virtue. Lean on human-heartedness. Take your recreation in the arts.”
The Master said: Set your heart on the Way. Hold fast to virtue. Lean on humaneness. And find your recreation in the arts.
The Master said, “No one has ever come to me with so much as a bundle of dried meat and gone away untaught.”
The Master said: From the man who brought no more than a bundle of dried meat for my teaching, I have never withheld instruction.

The Master said, “I do not open the door for a man who is not straining at it, or find the word for one who is not struggling to speak. I hold up one corner; if he cannot come back with the other three, I do not go on.”

The Master said: I do not open the way for one who is not burning to understand, nor help out one who is not struggling to put his thought into words. When I have shown a man one corner and he cannot come back to me with the other three, I do not go on.
When the Master ate beside a mourner, he never ate his fill. On a day he had wept, he did not sing.
When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill. On a day he had wept, he did not sing.

The Master said to Yen Yuan, “When wanted, to serve; when set aside, to withdraw — only you and I have that in us.” Tsze-lu said, “If you had command of the armies of a great state, whom would you take with you?” The Master said, “Not the man who would wrestle a tiger bare-handed or wade a river and die with no regrets. The man I take comes to the thing afraid, loves to plan, and carries the plan through.”

The Master said to Yen Yuan: To take up office when you are called, and to retire quietly when you are not — only you and I can do this. Tsze-lu said: If you had charge of the armies of a great state, whom would you take with you? The Master said: Not the man who would fight a tiger bare-handed or wade a river with no boat, and die without a second thought. The one I want is the one who comes to the work wary, who loves to lay his plans, and so brings them off.
The Master said, “If wealth could be had for the seeking, I would take up the whip and hold horses to get it. Since it cannot, I will follow what I love.”
The Master said: If riches could be had for the seeking, I would seek them, even with whip in hand as a groom. But since they cannot, I will follow what I love.
The things the Master treated with the greatest care were fasting, war, and sickness.
The things the Master treated with the most care were fasting, war, and sickness.
In Ch’i, the Master heard the Shao, and for three months he did not know the taste of meat. “I never imagined,” he said, “that music could be made as fine as this.”
When the Master was in Ch'i, he heard the Shao music, and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He said: I never imagined that music could reach such heights.

Yen Yu said, “Is our Master for the ruler of Wei?” Tsze-kung said, “Well — I will ask him.” He went in and said, “What sort of men were Po-i and Shu-ch’i?” “Worthies of the old days,” said the Master. “Did they regret how it ended for them?” “They sought human-heartedness and found it. What was there to regret?” Tsze-kung came out and said, “Our Master is not for him.”

Yen Yu said: Is the Master for the ruler of Wei? Tsze-kung said: I will go and ask him. He went in and said: What sort of men were Po-i and Shu-ch'i? The Master said: They were worthy men of old. And did they nurse any regret? The Master said: They sought humaneness, and they found it — what was there to regret? Tsze-kung came out and said: The Master is not for him.
The Master said, “Coarse rice to eat, water to drink, my bent arm for a pillow — there is joy in these things too. Wealth and rank that come by wrong are to me drifting clouds.”
The Master said: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow — even so I have joy. Riches and honor gotten by wrong are to me a passing cloud.
The Master said, “Give me a few more years — fifty for the study of the Yi — and I might come through without great faults.”
The Master said: Give me a few more years — fifty for the study of the Yi — and I might come through without grave faults.
The Master’s constant themes were the Odes, the History, and the keeping of ritual. Of these he never stopped speaking.
The Master often spoke of the Odes, the History, and the keeping of ritual. On these he spoke often.

The Duke of Sheh asked Tsze-lu about Confucius, and Tsze-lu gave him no answer. The Master said, “Why didn’t you say: he is a man so eager he forgets to eat, so glad he forgets every sorrow, and who has not noticed old age coming on?”

The Duke of Sheh asked Tsze-lu about Confucius, and Tsze-lu gave him no answer. The Master said: Why did you not simply tell him — here is a man who in his hunger for knowledge forgets to eat, who in his joy forgets his cares, and does not notice old age coming on?
The Master said, “I was not born knowing. I love what is old, and I go after it in earnest.”
The Master said: I am not one who was born knowing. I love the ancients, and I work hard to seek it there.
The Master did not speak of marvels, feats of strength, rebellion, or the spirits.
The Master did not talk of marvels, of feats of strength, of disorder, or of spirits.
The Master said, “Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher. I pick out what is good in them and follow it; what is bad, and mend it in myself.”
The Master said: Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher in them. I pick out what is good in them and follow it; what is bad, and mend it in myself.
The Master said, “Heaven planted this virtue in me. What can Hwan T’ui do to me?”
The Master said: Heaven planted the virtue that is in me. Hwan T'ui — what can he do to me?
The Master said, “Do you think I am hiding something, my friends? I hide nothing from you. There is nothing I do that is not laid open before you. That is who I am.”
The Master said: Do you think, my friends, that I keep anything back? I keep nothing back from you. There is nothing I do that I do not share with you — that is my way.
The Master taught four things: letters, conduct, loyalty, and good faith.
The Master taught four things: letters, conduct, faithfulness, and good faith.

The Master said, “A sage I will never get to see; a gentleman would be enough. A good man I will never get to see; a man of constancy would be enough. But men who have nothing and pose as having, who are empty and pose as full, who are pinched and pose as comfortable — constancy is beyond such men.”

The Master said: A sage I cannot hope to see; if I could see a person of real worth, that would be enough. The Master said: A good man I cannot hope to see; if I could see a man of constancy, that would be enough. To have nothing and act as if you had, to be empty and act as if you were full, to be in want and act as if you were at ease — it is hard for such a man to have constancy.
The Master angled, but never with a net. He shot, but never at a roosting bird.
The Master fished, but not with a net. He shot, but not at roosting birds.

The Master said, “There may be men who act without knowing why; I am not one of them. To hear much, choose what is good, and follow it; to see much and hold it in memory — that is the second kind of knowledge.”

The Master said: There may be those who act without knowing why; I am not one of them. To hear much, pick out the good, and follow it; to see much and hold it in mind — this is the next best thing to knowing.

The people of Hu-hsiang were hard to talk with, so when a boy from there was received, the disciples wondered. The Master said, “I take a man at his coming; I do not answer for what he does when he leaves. Why be so hard? If a man cleans himself to come to me, I receive him clean. I do not vouch for his past.”

The people of Hu-hsiang were hard to talk with, and when a boy from there was received by the Master, the disciples were uneasy. The Master said: I take a man as he comes to me; I do not answer for what he does once he leaves. Why be so harsh? When a man cleanses himself to come to me, I welcome the man he now is; I do not vouch for his past.
The Master said, “Is human-heartedness so far away? The moment I want it, it is here.”
The Master said: Is humaneness so far off? I want to be humane, and there — humaneness is here.

The minister of crime of Ch’an asked whether the duke Chao knew ritual, and Confucius said, “He knew ritual.” When Confucius had withdrawn, the minister beckoned Wu-ma Ch’i forward and said, “I have heard that a gentleman takes no side. Does a gentleman take sides after all? The prince took a wife from the house of Wu — his own surname — and covered it by calling her ‘The elder Tsze of Wu.’ If that prince knew ritual, who does not?” Wu-ma Ch’i passed this on, and the Master said, “I am a fortunate man. If I make a mistake, someone is sure to know it.”

The minister of crime of Ch'an asked whether Duke Chao knew ritual. Confucius said: He knew ritual. When Confucius had gone, the minister beckoned Wu-ma Ch'i forward and said: I had heard that the cultivated person takes no sides. Can he too take sides? The prince married a woman of the house of Wu, of his own surname, and called her "the elder Tsze of Wu." If this prince knew ritual, who does not? Wu-ma Ch'i reported this. The Master said: I am a lucky man. If I make a mistake, others are sure to know it.
When the Master was with a man who sang well, he would have him sing it again, and then join in.
When the Master was with someone who was singing and sang well, he would have him sing it again, and then join in.
The Master said, “In letters I am perhaps the equal of other men. As for living as a gentleman lives — carrying out in conduct what he professes — I have not yet arrived.”
The Master said: In letters I am perhaps no worse than other men. But to live out in my own conduct what the cultivated person professes — that I have not yet reached.

The Master said, “A sage? A man of human-heartedness? How would I dare? Say only this of me: I work toward it without tiring and teach without wearying — that much and no more.” Kung-hsi Hwa said, “And that much is exactly what we students cannot learn to do.”

The Master said: A sage, or a man of perfect humaneness — how could I dare claim to be either? But that I strive toward it without tiring, and teach others without weariness — that much may be said of me. Kung-hsi Hwa said: And that is just what we, your disciples, cannot learn to do.

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. The Master said, “Is that done?” Tsze-lu answered, “It is. The Eulogies say, ‘Prayer has been made for you to the spirits above and below.’” The Master said, “Then my praying began long ago.”

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. The Master said: Is there such a thing? Tsze-lu said: There is. The Eulogies say, "Prayer has been made for you to the spirits above and below." The Master said: Then my praying has been going on a long while.
The Master said, “Extravagance breeds arrogance; thrift breeds shabbiness. Better shabby than arrogant.”
The Master said: Extravagance breeds insolence, and stinginess breeds meanness. Better mean than insolent.
The Master said, “The gentleman is level and open; the small man is never out from under his cares.”
The Master said: The cultivated person is calm and at ease; the small man is always anxious and on edge.
The Master was mild, yet firm; imposing, yet not fierce; respectful, yet at ease.
The Master was gentle, yet firm; commanding, yet not harsh; respectful, yet at ease.

sections.label: Book VIII
sections.title: A Heavy Load, a Long Road
T'ai-po, and the Burden of the Scholar

segments.text: The Master said, “T’ai-po may be called virtue at its highest. Three times he gave up an empire, and he hid it so well the people could not even find words to praise him.”
The Master said: T'ai-po may be said to have reached the very height of virtue. Three times he gave up the empire, and so quietly that the people never even knew enough to praise him.

The Master said, “Respect without ritual is drudgery; caution without ritual is timidity; courage without ritual is disorder; honesty without ritual is a knife. When those in high place are devoted to their own kin, the people stir toward human-heartedness. When old friends are not dropped, the people do not turn cold.”

The Master said: Respectfulness without ritual becomes wearisome fuss; caution without ritual becomes timidity; boldness without ritual becomes rebellion; plain speaking without ritual becomes rudeness. When those in high place are devoted to their own kin, the people are stirred to humaneness; when they do not forget their old friends, the people are kept from meanness.

Master Tsang was ill. He called the disciples of his school and said, “Uncover my feet. Uncover my hands. The Odes say, ‘Trembling, watchful, as if at the edge of a deep gulf, as if treading on thin ice’ — and that is how I have lived. But from this moment, my little ones, I know that I have come through whole.”

Master Tsang was gravely ill, and called his disciples to him and said: Uncover my feet, uncover my hands. The Book of Poetry says, "In fear and trembling, as on the brink of a deep gulf, as treading thin ice." But now, my little children, I know that I have come through, my body whole.

Master Tsang was ill, and Meng Chang came to ask after him. Tsang said, “When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three things a gentleman holds precious in the Way: in his bearing, to keep far from violence and carelessness; in his face, to keep close to good faith; in his words and tone, to keep far from anything low or false. As for the sacrificial vessels, there are officers to mind them.”

Master Tsang was ill, and Meng Chang came to ask after him. Master Tsang said to him: When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three things the man of high rank should hold most important: that in his bearing and manner he keep clear of violence and carelessness; that in his looks he stay close to sincerity; and that in his words and tone he keep far from coarseness and impropriety. As for the sacrificial vessels, there are officers to see to those.

Master Tsang said, “Able, yet asking those less able; rich in knowledge, yet asking those with little; having, yet seeming to lack; full, yet counting himself empty; wronged, yet never striking back — I had a friend once who lived this way.”

Master Tsang said: Gifted, yet asking of those who were not; full of knowledge, yet asking of those who had little; having, yet as though he had not; full, yet counting himself empty; wronged, yet picking no quarrel — I once had a friend who lived like this.

Master Tsang said, “A man you could trust with an orphaned prince, a man you could charge with a state of a hundred li, a man no crisis however great can bend — is that a gentleman? That is a gentleman indeed.”

Master Tsang said: Suppose a man you could trust with a young orphaned prince, and charge with the rule of a domain of a hundred li, and whom no crisis, however great, could shake from his principles — is such a man a cultivated person? A cultivated person indeed.

Master Tsang said, “An officer cannot go without breadth and staying power. The load is heavy and the road is long. Human-heartedness is the load he carries — is that not heavy? Only death ends the road — is that not long?”

Master Tsang said: The scholar cannot be without breadth of mind and tough endurance, for his burden is heavy and his road is long. Humaneness is the burden he takes as his own — is it not heavy? Only with death does the road end — is it not long?
The Master said, “The Odes wake us. Ritual sets us on our feet. Music finishes the work.”
The Master said: Roused by the Odes; established by ritual; perfected by music.
The Master said, “The people can be made to follow the Way; they cannot be made to understand it.”
The Master said: The people may be made to follow a path, but not to understand it.
The Master said, “A man who loves daring and resents his poverty will make disorder. So will a man without human-heartedness, if you press your hatred of him too far.”
