The Master said, "In the drawing up of a state paper, P'i Shan made the rough draft, Shi-shu examined and discussed it, Tsze-yu, the master of embassies, polished it, and Tsze-ch'an of Tung-li gave it its finish."

The Master said: In drawing up the state's proclamations, P'i Shan made the rough draft; Shi-shu went over it and weighed its contents; Tsze-yu, who managed foreign affairs, polished the wording; and Tsze-ch'an of Tung-li gave it grace and finish.

Someone asked about Tsze-ch'an. The Master said, "A generous man." He asked about Tsze-hsi. "That man! That man!" He asked about Kwan Chung. The Master said, "He was a man: Pien, a town of three hundred households, was taken from the head of the Po family for him, and the Po chief, brought down to coarse rice, never let one resentful word be heard to the end of his life."

Someone asked about Tsze-ch'an. The Master said: A kind man. He asked about Tsze-hsi. The Master said: That man! That man! He asked about Kwan Chung. The Master said: This is a man who stripped the head of the Po family of the town of Pien with its three hundred households — and to the end of his days, eating only coarse rice, the man never spoke a word of complaint.
The Master said, "To be poor without resentment is hard. To be rich without arrogance is easy."
The Master said: To be poor and not complain is hard. To be rich and not proud is easy.
The Master said, "Mang Kung-ch'o would make a fine elder for the house of Chao or Wei; but he could not serve as a great officer of Tang or Hsieh."
The Master said: Mang Kung-ch'o is more than fit to be steward to great houses like Chao and Wei, but he is not fit to be a minister in a small state like Tang or Hsieh.

Tsze-lu asked what makes a complete man. The Master said, "Take the knowledge of Tsang Wu-chung, the freedom from greed of Kung-ch'o, the bravery of Chwang of Pien, and the many talents of Zan Ch'iu, and finish them with ritual and music — that might be called a complete man." Then he said, "But need a complete man of these days have all that? A man who at the sight of gain thinks of what is right; who at the sight of danger is ready to give his life; who does not forget the promise of years ago, however long the years — he too may be called a complete man."

Tsze-lu asked what makes a complete man. The Master said: Take the wisdom of Tsang Wu-chung, the freedom from greed of Kung-ch'o, the courage of Chwang of Pien, and the many talents of Zan Ch'iu, and round them off with ritual and music — such a one might be called a complete man. Then he added: But why must a complete man today be all of that? The man who, seeing a chance for gain, thinks of what is right; who, seeing danger, is ready to give his life; and who does not forget an old promise, however far back it was made — such a man too may be called complete.

The Master asked Kung-ming Chia about Kung-shu Wan: "Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not take?" Kung-ming Chia answered, "Whoever told you that told you too much. My master speaks when it is time to speak, so no one tires of his speaking. He laughs when there is something to be glad of, so no one tires of his laughing. He takes when taking is right, so no one tires of his taking." The Master said, "So? Can it really be so?"

The Master asked Kung-ming Chia about Kung-shu Wan, saying: Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not take? Kung-ming Chia replied: Whoever told you that went too far. My master speaks when it is time to speak, so men never tire of his speaking. He laughs when there is reason for joy, so men never tire of his laughing. He takes only when it is right to take, so men never tire of his taking. The Master said: Is that so? Can it really be so with him?
The Master said, "Tsang Wu-chung held the city of Fang while he asked the duke of Lu to appoint his heir. Say what you like about his not coercing his prince — I do not believe it."
The Master said: Tsang Wu-chung, holding the town of Fang, pressed the Duke of Lu to name a successor to his family. They say he did not force his ruler in this — but I believe he did.
The Master said, "Duke Wan of Tsin was crafty and not straight. Duke Hwan of Ch'i was straight and not crafty."
The Master said: Duke Wan of Tsin was crafty and not upright. Duke Hwan of Ch'i was upright and not crafty.

Tsze-lu said, "When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Shao Hu died with his master. Kwan Chung did not. Was that not a failure of human-heartedness?" The Master said, "That Duke Hwan could gather all the princes together, and not by war-chariots and weapons — that was Kwan Chung's strength. Where is the human-heartedness to match his! Where is the human-heartedness to match his!"

Tsze-lu said: When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Shao Hu died with their master, but Kwan Chung did not die. May I not say he fell short of humaneness? The Master said: Duke Hwan brought all the princes together nine times, and not by force of chariots and arms — this was the work of Kwan Chung. Such was his humaneness! Such was his humaneness!

Tsze-kung said, "Kwan Chung was no human-hearted man, surely? When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Kwan Chung could not even die with him — he went on to serve as Hwan's prime minister." The Master said, "Kwan Chung served as minister to Duke Hwan, made him chief of all the princes, and set the whole kingdom in order — and the people are living on his gifts to this day. But for Kwan Chung, we would be wearing our hair loose and buttoning our coats on the left. Would you have him keep the small good faith of a common man and his wife — strangled in some ditch, and no one ever the wiser?"

Tsze-kung said: Kwan Chung, I think, fell short of humaneness. When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Kwan Chung could not bring himself to die with him — and more, he became Hwan's prime minister. The Master said: Kwan Chung served as Duke Hwan's prime minister, made him leader of all the princes, and set the whole kingdom right; to this day the people enjoy what he gave them. But for Kwan Chung, we would be wearing our hair loose and folding our coats to the left. Would you have him keep the petty good faith of common men and women, who hang themselves in a ditch and no one ever the wiser?
Kung-shu Wan's own steward, the great officer Hsien, rose to the prince's court at Wan's side. When the Master heard of it, he said, "He deserved to be called Wan — 'the cultured.'"
Hsien, the steward who had served Kung-shu Wan, went up to the prince's court at his master's side. When the Master heard of it, he said: He earned the name Wan — the accomplished.

The Master was speaking of the misrule of Duke Ling of Wei, and Chi K'ang said, "If he is such a man, how is it he does not lose his state?" Confucius said, "Chung-shu Yu looks after his guests and envoys, the litanist T'o keeps his ancestral temple, and Wang-sun Chia commands his army. With officers like those, how should he lose his state?"

The Master was speaking of the misrule of Duke Ling of Wei, when Ch'i K'ang said: If he is like that, how does he not lose his state? Confucius said: Chung-shu Yu has charge of his guests and strangers, the priest T'o has charge of his ancestral temple, and Wang-sun Chia has charge of the army. With officers like these, how would he lose his state?
The Master said, "Say a thing without a blush, and you will find it hard to make the thing good."
The Master said: A man who makes his claims without modesty will find them hard to make good.

Chan Ch'ang murdered Duke Chien of Ch'i. Confucius bathed, went to court, and told Duke Ai, "Chan Hang has slain his sovereign. I ask you to punish him." The duke said, "Tell the chiefs of the three families." Confucius withdrew, saying, "Because I walk behind the great officers, I did not dare not to speak. And my prince says, 'Tell the chiefs of the three families.'" He went and told the chiefs, and they refused. Confucius said, "Because I walk behind the great officers, I did not dare not to speak."

Chan Ch'ang murdered Duke Chien of Ch'i. Confucius bathed, went to court, and reported to Duke Ai: Chan Hang has slain his ruler. I beg you to punish him. The Duke said: Tell the chiefs of the three families. Confucius withdrew and said: Coming after the great officers, I did not dare to leave such a thing unreported — and my prince says, "Tell the three families." He went to the three families and reported it, and they would not act. Confucius said: Coming after the great officers, I did not dare to leave such a thing unreported.
Tsze-lu asked how to serve a ruler. The Master said, "Never deceive him. And stand up to his face."
Tsze-lu asked how to serve a ruler. The Master said: Do not deceive him — and do stand up to him to his face.
The Master said, "The gentleman works his way upward. The small man works his way down."
The Master said: The cultivated person makes his way upward; the small man makes his way downward.
The Master said, "The men of old learned for their own sake. The men of today learn for the eyes of others."
The Master said: In old times men learned for their own sake; nowadays men learn to impress others.

Chu Po-yu sent a man to Confucius with his greetings. Confucius sat with him and asked, "What is your master working at?" The messenger answered, "My master wants to make his faults fewer, and has not yet managed it." When he had gone out, the Master said, "There is a messenger! There is a messenger!"

Chu Po-yu sent a messenger with kind inquiries to Confucius. Confucius sat him down and asked: What is your master busy with? The messenger replied: My master longs to make his faults few, but he has not yet managed it. When the messenger had gone out, the Master said: A messenger indeed! A messenger indeed!
The Master said, "If the office is not yours, its policies are not your business."
The Master said: A man who does not hold a given office should not meddle in its business.
Master Tsang said, "The gentleman's thoughts do not wander from his post."
Master Tsang said: The cultivated person, in his thoughts, does not stray beyond his place.
The Master said, "The gentleman is ashamed to let his words outrun his deeds."
The Master said: The cultivated person is modest in his words and outdoes them in his deeds.

The Master said, "The Way of the gentleman runs three ways, and I can manage none of them: human-hearted, he is free of care; wise, he is free of confusion; brave, he is free of fear." Tsze-kung said, "Master, you have just described yourself."

The Master said: The way of the cultivated person is threefold, and I fall short of all three: humane, he is free of anxiety; wise, he is free of confusion; brave, he is free of fear. Tsze-kung said: Master, that is your own portrait.
Tsze-kung was always measuring men against one another. The Master said, "Ts'ze must be a worthy man indeed. I have no time to spare for that."
Tsze-kung was given to weighing other men against each other. The Master said: Ts'ze must have reached great heights! I myself have no time to spare for that.
The Master said, "I am not troubled that men do not know me. I am troubled by my own want of ability."
The Master said: I will not worry that others do not know me; I will worry that I am not able.
The Master said, "Not to expect deceit, not to imagine bad faith — and yet to be the first to sense them when they come: is that not a worthy man?"

The Master said: Not to guard beforehand against being deceived, nor to suspect beforehand that you will not be trusted, and yet to see these things coming the moment they appear — is that not the mark of a person of worth?

Wei-shang Mau said to Confucius, "Ch'iu, what is all this perching here and roosting there? Have you become a smooth talker?" Confucius said, "I would not dare to be a smooth talker. But I hate a man who will not budge."

Wei-shang Mau said to Confucius: Ch'iu, why do you keep perching here and there like this? Are you not a smooth-tongued talker? Confucius said: I would not dare play the smooth talker — but I do hate stubbornness.
The Master said, "A ch'i is not called a great horse for its strength, but for its virtue."
The Master said: A fine horse is praised not for its strength but for its character.
Someone said, "What do you say of repaying injury with kindness?" The Master said, "Then what will you repay kindness with? Repay injury with straight justice. Repay kindness with kindness."
Someone said: What of the saying that injury should be repaid with kindness? The Master said: Then with what will you repay kindness? Repay injury with uprightness, and repay kindness with kindness.

The Master said, "No one knows me — alas!" Tsze-kung said, "Why do you say no one knows you?" The Master said, "I do not rail at Heaven. I do not blame men. I learn from what is lowest and reach toward what is highest. And the one who knows me — is that not Heaven?"

The Master said: Alas, no one knows me! Tsze-kung said: What do you mean — no one knows you? The Master said: I make no complaint against Heaven, I lay no blame on men. My studies are of low and common things, and my understanding reaches to the heights. The one who knows me — is that not Heaven?

Kung-po Liao slandered Tsze-lu to Chi-sun. Tsze-fu Ching-po brought word of it, saying, "My master's mind is certainly being poisoned by Kung-po Liao — but I still have power enough to see Liao's corpse exposed in the market and the court." The Master said, "If the Way is to go forward, that is the decree. If the Way is to fall, that is the decree too. What can Kung-po Liao do against the decree?"

Kung-po Liao had slandered Tsze-lu to Chi-sun. Tsze-fu Ching-po brought word of it to Confucius, saying: My lord is certainly being led astray by Kung-po Liao, but I still have the power to have Liao cut down and his corpse displayed in the marketplace. The Master said: Whether my Way is to go forward, that is fate. Whether it is to come to nothing, that is fate. What can Kung-po Liao do against fate?
The Master said, "Some worthy men withdraw from the world. Some withdraw from a state. Some withdraw at a look. Some withdraw at a word."
The Master said: Some men of worth withdraw from the world; some withdraw from a particular state; some withdraw at the first slighting look; some withdraw at the first word of insult.
The Master said, "Seven men have done so."
The Master said: Those who did this were seven men.
Tsze-lu passed a night in Shih-man. The gatekeeper asked, "From whom do you come?" "From Mr. K'ung." "Ah," said the gatekeeper, "the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on doing it?"
Tsze-lu spent a night at Shih-man. The gatekeeper said: Where do you come from? Tsze-lu said: From the house of K'ung. The man said: Is that the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on trying?

One day in Wei the Master was playing the stone chimes, when a man carrying a straw basket passed the door and said, "There is a heart still full of the world, in that beating of stones!" Then he added, "But how petty, that stubborn clang-clang! If no one knows you, give it up, and be done. 'Where the water is deep, wade through in your clothes; where it is shallow, hitch them up.'" The Master said, "How resolute! Giving up — there is nothing hard in that."

The Master was beating the stone chimes one day in Wei, when a man carrying a straw basket passed the door and said: There is a full heart in the way he strikes those chimes! After a while he added: How petty this stubborn clanging is! If no one takes any notice of you, then have done with it. "Where the water is deep, wade through clothes and all; where it is shallow, hold your skirts up and cross." The Master said: How firmly set he is — there is no answering that!

Tsze-chang said, "The Book of History says that Kao-tsung kept the royal mourning three years without speaking. What does that mean?" The Master said, "Why single out Kao-tsung? The ancients all did the same. When a sovereign died, the officers of state gathered their duties and answered to the prime minister for three years."

Tsze-chang said: What does the Book of History mean when it says that Kao-tsung, in the mourning hut, did not speak for three years? The Master said: Why single out Kao-tsung? All the ancients did the same. When the ruler died, the officers each kept to their posts and took their orders from the prime minister for three years.
The Master said, "When those above love ritual, the people are easy to lead."
The Master said: When those above love ritual, the people are easy to command.

Tsze-lu asked about the gentleman. The Master said, "He cultivates himself into reverent care." "Is that all?" "He cultivates himself, and others find rest in him." "Is that all?" "He cultivates himself, and the whole people find rest in him. He cultivates himself, and the whole people find rest — even Yao and Shun found that past their strength."

Tsze-lu asked what makes a cultivated person. The Master said: He cultivates himself to become reverent and careful. Is that all? asked Tsze-lu. He cultivates himself so as to bring rest to others. Is that all? asked Tsze-lu. The Master said: He cultivates himself so as to bring rest to all the people. To cultivate yourself so as to bring rest to all the people — even Yao and Shun found that hard.

Yuan Zang sat sprawled on his heels, waiting for the Master, who said to him, "Young, and never modest; grown, and nothing to your name; old, and refusing to die — you are a pest." And he rapped him on the shin with his staff.

Yuan Zang sat sprawling on his heels, waiting for the Master, who said: As a boy, no respect for your elders; grown up, nothing worth handing down; and old now, and still not dead — you are a pest. And with that he rapped him on the shin with his staff.

A boy of the village of Ch'ueh used to carry messages between the Master and his visitors. Someone asked about him: "Coming along well, I suppose?" The Master said, "I have seen him take a grown man's seat, and I have seen him walk abreast of his elders. He is not after progress. He is in a hurry to be finished."

A boy of the village of Ch'ueh was carrying messages for Confucius. Someone asked about him: Is he one who is making real progress? The Master said: I see him take the seat meant for a grown man, and walk shoulder to shoulder with his elders. He is not after progress; he wants to be a man before his time.

Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius about the ordering of troops. Confucius answered, "Matters of sacrificial vessels I have heard something of. Matters of armies I have never studied." The next day he took his leave. In Ch'an the provisions ran out, and his followers grew too sick to stand. Tsze-lu came to him with his anger showing: "So the gentleman, too, can be brought to this?" The Master said, "A gentleman holds firm in want. A small man in want runs over like flood water."

Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius about battle formations. Confucius answered: I have learned about the vessels of sacrifice, but I have never studied warfare. The next day he left. In Ch'an the provisions ran out, and his followers grew so weak they could not get to their feet. Tsze-lu, plainly aggrieved, said: Must the cultivated person endure such want as this? The Master said: The cultivated person endures want and holds firm; the small man, in want, breaks loose into license.

The Master said, "Ts'ze, you take me for a man who has studied much and holds it all in memory?" "Yes," he answered. "Is it not so?" "No," said the Master. "I have one thread, and everything is strung on it."
The Master said: Ts'ze, you take me, I suppose, for one who learns many things and holds them all in mind? He answered: Yes — is that not so? No, said the Master: I thread it all on a single thread.
The Master said, "Yu, the men who know virtue are few."
The Master said: Yu, how few are those who understand virtue.
The Master said, "If any man governed without governing, it was Shun. What did he do? He composed himself in reverence and sat facing due south — that is all."
The Master said: Was it not Shun who ruled by doing nothing? For what did he do? He composed himself in reverence and faced south, and that was all.

Tsze-chang asked how a man should act, that his way be open wherever he goes. The Master said, "Let his words be loyal and true, his conduct earnest and careful, and his way will be open even in the lands of the wild tribes, south or north. Let his words be disloyal and false, his conduct careless and cold — will his way be open even in his own district? Standing, see these two things ranged in front of you. Riding, see them leaning on the yoke. Then your way will be open." Tsze-chang wrote the words on his sash.

Tsze-chang asked how a man should carry himself to get on everywhere. The Master said: Let his words be faithful and true, his actions honest and careful, and he will get on even among the rude tribes of the south and north. Let his words be neither faithful nor true, his actions neither honest nor careful, and will he get on even in his own neighborhood? When you stand, see these words ranged before you; when you ride, see them resting on the yoke. Then you may carry them into practice. Tsze-chang wrote them on the end of his sash.

The Master said, "Straight — that was the historian Yu! When the state kept the Way, he was an arrow. When the state lost the Way, he was an arrow. And a gentleman — that is Chu Po-yu! When the state keeps the Way, he serves. When the state loses it, he can roll his Way up and put it away inside his coat."

The Master said: Straight indeed was the recorder Yu! When the state had good government, he was an arrow; when it had bad government, he was an arrow still. A cultivated person indeed is Chu Po-yu! When the state had good government, he took office; when it had bad government, he could roll up his principles and keep them in his breast.
The Master said, "To fail to speak with a man worth speaking to is to waste the man. To speak with a man not worth speaking to is to waste your words. The wise waste neither men nor words."

The Master said: When a man is worth speaking to, and you do not speak to him, you lose the man. When a man is not worth speaking to, and you speak to him, you waste your words. The wise lose neither the man nor their words.

The Master said, "The scholar with a purpose, the man of human-heartedness — they will not cling to life at the cost of human-heartedness. There are times when they will give the body to death to bring it whole."
The Master said: The scholar set on his purpose, and the humane man, will not seek life at the cost of their humaneness; there are times they will give their lives to keep their humaneness whole.

Tsze-kung asked how to work at human-heartedness. The Master said, "A craftsman who wants his work good sharpens his tools first. Whatever state you live in, serve the worthiest of its great officers, and make friends with the most human-hearted of its scholars."

Tsze-kung asked about the practice of humaneness. The Master said: A workman who would do his work well must first sharpen his tools. Living in a state, take service under the worthiest of its ministers, and make friends of the most humane among its scholars.

Yen Yuan asked how a state should be run. The Master said, "Keep the calendar of Hsia. Ride the plain state carriage of Yin. Wear the ceremonial cap of Chau. For music, the Shao and its dances. Banish the tunes of Chang, and keep clever talkers at a distance — the tunes of Chang are wanton, and clever talkers are dangerous."

Yen Yuan asked how a country should be governed. The Master said: Keep the seasons of the Hsia. Ride in the carriage of the Yin. Wear the cap of the Chau. For music, the Shao with its dances. Banish the tunes of Chang and keep glib talkers at a distance; the tunes of Chang are licentious, and glib talkers are dangerous.
The Master said, "A man who gives no thought to what is far off will find his sorrow near at hand."
The Master said: A man who gives no thought to what is far off will find his troubles close at hand.
The Master said, "It is finished! I have yet to meet the man who loves virtue the way he loves beauty."
The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to see a man who loved virtue as he loves a beautiful face.
The Master said, "Did Tsang Wan not hold his post like a thief? He knew the worth of Hui of Liu-hsia, and did not raise him to stand at his side in court."
The Master said: Did not Tsang Wan steal his post? He knew the worth of Hui of Liu-hsia, and yet would not stand him beside himself at court.
The Master said, "Demand much of yourself, and little of others, and resentment will keep its distance."
The Master said: Demand much of yourself, little of others, and you will keep resentment far off.
The Master said, "A man who never asks himself, 'What am I to make of this? What am I to make of this?' — I can make nothing of him."
The Master said: A man who never asks himself, "How shall I handle this? How shall I handle this?" — with such a man there is nothing I can do.
The Master said, "Together the whole day, their talk never once touching what is right, and delighting in little feats of cleverness — hard cases indeed!"
The Master said: A whole day together, and not a word of their talk touches on what is right, while they delight in showing off small cleverness — there is no helping such men.
The Master said, "What is right is the gentleman's substance. Ritual is how he carries it out, humility is how he brings it forward, good faith is how he completes it. That is a gentleman."

The Master said: The cultivated person takes what is right as the ground of all he does. He carries it out with ritual, brings it forth in humility, and completes it in good faith. That is the cultivated person.
The Master said, "The gentleman is pained by his own want of ability. He is not pained that men do not know him."
The Master said: The cultivated person is distressed by his own incapacity; he is not distressed that others fail to know him.
The Master said, "The gentleman dreads leaving the world with his name unspoken."
The Master said: The cultivated person hates the thought of leaving the world with his name unspoken.
The Master said, "The gentleman makes his demands of himself. The small man makes his demands of others."
The Master said: The cultivated person seeks it in himself; the small man seeks it in others.
The Master said, "The gentleman holds his ground, and does not wrangle. He keeps company, and joins no faction."
The Master said: The cultivated person has self-respect and does not quarrel; he keeps company with others and joins no faction.
The Master said, "The gentleman does not raise a man up because of his words, and he does not throw away words because of the man."
The Master said: The cultivated person does not raise a man up for his words alone, nor throw out good words because of the man who speaks them.
Tsze-kung asked, "Is there one word a man could walk with all his life?" The Master said, "Would that not be reciprocity? What you do not want done to you, do not do to others."
Tsze-kung asked: Is there a single word one can practice all one's life? The Master said: Is it not reciprocity? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.

The Master said, "Of the men I deal with, whom do I blame beyond his due, and whom do I praise beyond it? If I have ever praised a man too high, he had been put to the proof first. It was with this same people that the three dynasties kept to the straight road."

The Master said: In my dealings with men, whose evil have I blamed, whose good have I praised, beyond what was deserved? If I have praised any beyond their due, there was ground for it once I had looked into the man. This is the people through whom the three dynasties held to their straight course.
The Master said, "I am old enough to remember when a scribe would leave a blank where he was unsure, and a man with a horse would lend it to a neighbor to ride. Now even that much is gone."
The Master said: Even in my own day a recorder would leave a blank where he was unsure, and a man with a horse would lend it to another to ride. Now even that is gone.
The Master said, "Clever words throw virtue into confusion. Impatience in a small thing throws a great plan into ruin."
The Master said: Clever words confound virtue; a little impatience confounds great plans.
The Master said, "When the crowd hates a man, look into it. When the crowd loves a man, look into it."
The Master said: When the many hate a man, look into it for yourself; when the many love a man, look into it for yourself.
The Master said, "A man can make the Way great. The Way does not make the man great."
The Master said: A man can enlarge the Way; the Way does not enlarge the man.
The Master said, "To have a fault and not mend it — that is what deserves to be called a fault."
The Master said: To err and not mend it — that is to err indeed.
The Master said, "I have gone a whole day without food and a whole night without sleep, to think. It came to nothing. Better to learn."
The Master said: Once I went a whole day without food and a whole night without sleep, given over to thought. It came to nothing. Better to learn.

The Master said, "The gentleman lays his plans for the Way, not for his food. Plow, and hunger can lie in the middle of it; learn, and pay can lie in the middle of it. The gentleman worries about the Way. He does not worry about being poor."

The Master said: The cultivated person sets his mind on the Way, not on his food. Take to farming, and hunger may still find you; take to learning, and a salary may follow. The cultivated person worries about the Way, not about poverty.

The Master said, "What wisdom reaches, human-heartedness must hold; otherwise, though a man gains it, he will lose it again. What wisdom reaches and human-heartedness holds, he must preside over with dignity, or the people will not respect him. And what wisdom reaches, human-heartedness holds, and dignity presides over, he must still set in motion by ritual. Short of that, it is not yet good."

The Master said: Knowledge enough to reach it, but not virtue enough to hold it — what you gain, you will lose again. Knowledge enough to reach it, virtue enough to hold it, but no dignity in governing — and the people will not respect you. Knowledge enough to reach it, virtue enough to hold it, dignity in governing — but if you set the people moving against ritual, it is still not good enough.
The Master said, "The gentleman cannot be read in small things, but he can be trusted with great ones. The small man cannot be trusted with great things, but he can be read in small ones."
The Master said: The cultivated person cannot be known in small things, but may be entrusted with great ones; the small man cannot be entrusted with great things, but may be known in small ones.

The Master said, "Human-heartedness matters more to the people than water and fire. I have seen men die from stepping into water and fire. I have never seen a man die from stepping into human-heartedness."
The Master said: Humaneness is more to the people than water and fire. I have seen men die from treading on water and fire; I have never seen a man die from treading the path of humaneness.
The Master said, "When it comes to human-heartedness, do not yield place — not even to your teacher."
The Master said: Where humaneness is at stake, give way to no one, not even your teacher.
The Master said, "The gentleman is firm in the right; he is not blindly bound by his word."
The Master said: The cultivated person is firm where it is right, not stubborn for its own sake.
The Master said, "In serving your prince, be exacting about the work. Let the pay come after."
The Master said: In serving his ruler, a man should attend to his duties first and put his pay second.
The Master said, "In teaching, there are no classes of men."
The Master said: In teaching there are no classes of men.
The Master said, "Men whose Ways are different cannot make plans together."
The Master said: Those who walk by different ways cannot lay plans together.
The Master said, "Words are for reaching the meaning. That is all."
The Master said: In speech, all that is asked is that it carry the meaning.

Mien, the music-master, came to call. When they reached the steps, the Master said, "Here are the steps." When they reached the mat, the Master said, "Here is the mat." When everyone was seated, the Master told him, "So-and-so is here. So-and-so is there." After the music-master had gone, Tsze-chang asked, "Is that the way to speak with a music-master?" The Master said, "Yes. That is exactly how one helps the blind."

The music-master Mien came to call. When they reached the steps, the Master said: Here are the steps. When they reached the mat, he said: Here is the mat. When all were seated, he told him: So-and-so is here, so-and-so is there. After the music-master Mien had gone, Tsze-chang asked: Is that the way to speak with a music-master? The Master said: Yes. That is certainly the way to help the blind.

sections.label: Book XVI
sections.title: The Chi Family
The Chi Family, and the Numbered Lists

segments.text: The head of the Chi family was about to attack Chwan-yu. Zan Yu and Chi-lu came to see Confucius and said, "Our chief is going to move against Chwan-yu." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, isn't this your failure? Long ago a former king gave the ruler of Chwan-yu charge of the sacrifices to the eastern Mang. Besides, the place lies inside our own borders, and its lord is a minister of the sovereign himself. What business has your chief attacking it?" Zan Yu said, "Our master wants this. Neither of us, his two ministers, wants it." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, Chau Zan had a saying: 'Show your strength and take your place in the ranks; if you cannot, step down.' What good is a guide who won't steady the blind man when he totters, or lift him when he falls? And besides, what you say is wrong. When the tiger or the rhinoceros breaks out of its cage, when the tortoise-shell or the jade is smashed inside its case — whose fault is that?" Zan Yu said, "But Chwan-yu is strong now, and close to Pi. If our chief does not take it today, it will be a grief to his sons and grandsons." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, a gentleman hates the man who will not say plainly 'I want it,' and has to dress the wanting up in reasons. Here is what I have heard: the lord of a state, the head of a house, does not worry that his people are few; he worries that what they have is shared unevenly. He does not worry about poverty; he worries about unrest. For share evenly, and there is no poverty; live in harmony, and there is no lack of people; keep the peace, and nothing gets overthrown."

The head of the Chi family was about to attack Chwan-yu. Zan Yu and Tsze-lu came to see Confucius and said: Our chief, Chi, is about to move against Chwan-yu. Confucius said: Ch'iu, is this not your fault? Long ago a former king gave the ruler of Chwan-yu charge over the sacrifices to the eastern Mang; besides, it lies within our own borders, and its ruler holds his office directly from the crown. What has your chief to do with attacking it? Zan Yu said: Our master wishes it; neither of us two wishes it. Confucius said: Ch'iu, Chau Zan had a saying — "He who can put forth his strength takes his place in the ranks of office; he who cannot, steps down." What use is a guide to a blind man who does not steady him when he totters, nor lift him up when he falls? And more — you speak wrongly. When the tiger or the wild ox breaks out of its cage, when the tortoise-shell or the jade is smashed in its case, whose fault is that? Zan Yu said: But Chwan-yu is strong now, and close to Pi; if our chief does not take it now, it will be a grief to his descendants. Confucius said: Ch'iu, the cultivated person despises the man who will not plainly say "I want this," and then trumps up reasons for it. This I have heard: that the lord of a state or the head of a house frets not over having few people, but over their not keeping their places; not over poverty, but over unrest. For where each keeps his place there is no poverty; where there is harmony there is no lack of people; where there is peace, there is no overthrow. And so, if those far off will not submit, you draw them by cultivating the ways of culture and virtue, and once they have come, you make them content. Now here are you, Yu and Ch'iu, helping your chief — and those far off will not submit, and you cannot draw them; the state itself is splitting and falling apart, and you cannot hold it together; and yet you plot to take up arms within its own borders. I fear that the grief of the Chi-sun family will not come from Chwan-yu, but from within the screen of their own court.

"And so, if people far away will not submit, you cultivate learning and virtue to draw them in — and once they have come, you give them peace. Now look at the two of you, Yu and Ch'iu, standing at your chief's side. People far away will not submit, and you cannot draw them in. The state itself is splitting and crumbling, and you cannot hold it together. And in the middle of this, he plans to raise spears and shields inside his own country. I am afraid the trouble of the Chi-sun family is not coming from Chwan-yu. It is waiting inside their own walls."

Confucius said: When the Way prevails in the world, ritual, music, and the order to make war come from the son of Heaven. When the Way does not prevail, they come from the princes; and when they come from the princes, rarely will such a house keep its power past ten generations. When they come from the great officers, rarely will it keep its power past five generations. When the under-stewards of the great officers hold the orders of the state in their grasp, rarely will they keep their power past three generations. When the Way prevails in the world, government is not in the hands of the great officers. When the Way prevails in the world, the common people do not argue over it.

Confucius said, "When the Way holds in the world, ritual, music, and military campaigns issue from the Son of Heaven. When the Way is lost, they issue from the princes — and once they issue from the princes, few houses last ten generations. Once they issue from the great officers, few last five. Once the stewards of the great officers hold the orders of state in their hands, few last three. When the Way holds in the world, government does not sit with the great officers. When the Way holds in the world, the common people do not argue politics."

Confucius said: The revenue has been out of the ducal house now for five generations, and government has been in the hands of the great officers for four. That is why the descendants of the three Hwan have come so low.

Confucius said, "The revenue left the ducal house five generations ago. The government has sat with the great officers for four. That is why the descendants of the three Hwan are fading away." Confucius said, "Three friendships profit a man, and three do him harm. Friendship with the upright, friendship with the faithful, friendship with the widely informed — these profit him. Friendship with the man of studied airs, friendship with the professional pleaser, friendship with the glib — these do him harm."

Confucius said: There are three friendships that help and three that harm. Friendship with the upright, with the sincere, and with the man of wide learning — these help. Friendship with the plausible, with the soft flatterer, and with the glib-tongued — these harm.

Confucius said, "Three pleasures profit a man, and three do him harm. Pleasure in the measured practice of ritual and music, pleasure in speaking well of others, pleasure in having many worthy friends — these profit him. Pleasure in extravagance, pleasure in idle roaming, pleasure in the feast — these do him harm." Confucius said, "In attendance on a gentleman, there are three mistakes. To speak before it is your turn — that is called rashness. To hold back when it is your turn — that is called hiding. To speak without reading his face — that is called blindness."

Confucius said: There are three enjoyments that help and three that harm. To take joy in the right ordering of ritual and music, to take joy in speaking of the good in others, to take joy in having many worthy friends — these help. To take joy in reckless pleasure, to take joy in idle loafing, to take joy in feasting — these harm.

Confucius said, "There are three things a gentleman guards against. In youth, before the blood has settled, he guards against lust. In his prime, when the blood is at full strength, he guards against fighting. In old age, when the blood has thinned, he guards against greed." Confucius said, "There are three things a gentleman stands in awe of. He stands in awe of Heaven's decrees. He stands in awe of great men. He stands in awe of the words of the sages. The small man does not know Heaven's decrees, and so does not fear them. He takes liberties with great men. He makes jokes of the words of the sages."

Confucius said: In waiting on a man of virtue and rank there are three errors. To speak before it is your turn — that is rashness. To stay silent when it is your turn — that is concealment. To speak without watching his face — that is blindness.

Confucius said, "Those born knowing it stand highest. Those who learn it and come to know stand next. Those who find it hard and learn anyway come after them. Those who find it hard and do not learn — they are the lowest of the people." Confucius said, "A gentleman keeps nine things in mind. Seeing, he thinks: is it clear? Hearing: is it exact? His expression: is it warm? His bearing: is it respectful? His words: are they true? His work: is it careful? In doubt, he thinks of asking. In anger, he thinks of the trouble to come. And at the sight of gain, he thinks of what is right."

Confucius said: There are three things the cultivated person guards against. In youth, when the blood and vital powers are unsettled, he guards against lust. In his prime, when blood and vigor run full, he guards against quarreling. In age, when blood and vigor have waned, he guards against greed.

Confucius said, "'They see the good and chase it as if they could never catch up; they see the bad and flinch as if they had put a hand in boiling water' — I have seen the men, and I have heard the words. 'They live hidden to pursue their aims; they do what is right to carry their Way through' — I have heard the words. I have not seen the men." The duke Ching of Ch'i had a thousand teams of four horses; the day he died, the people could not find one virtue to praise him for. Po-i and Shu-ch'i starved to death at the foot of Shau-yang mountain, and the people praise them to this day. Isn't that what the saying means?

Confucius said: There are three things the cultivated person stands in awe of. He stands in awe of the will of Heaven, in awe of great men, in awe of the words of the sages. The small man does not know the will of Heaven and so holds it in no awe; he is rude to great men, and makes a mockery of the words of the sages.

Ch'an K'ang asked Po-yu, "Have you heard anything from your father that the rest of us have not?" Po-yu answered, "No. Once, when he was standing alone and I hurried across the courtyard, he said to me, 'Have you learned the Odes?' 'Not yet,' I said. 'If you do not learn the Odes,' he said, 'you will have nothing to say.' I went away and studied the Odes."

Confucius said: Those born with knowledge are the highest. Next come those who learn and so come to it. Next after them are the slow who learn for all that. And the slow who will not learn — they are the lowest of the people.

"Another day he was standing alone again, and as I hurried across the courtyard he said to me, 'Have you learned ritual?' 'Not yet,' I said. 'If you do not learn ritual,' he said, 'you will have nothing to stand on.' I went away and studied ritual. Those two things are all I have ever heard from him." Ch'an K'ang came away delighted. "I asked one thing," he said, "and I have gotten three. I have heard about the Odes. I have heard about ritual. And I have heard that a gentleman keeps his own son at arm's length."

Confucius said: The cultivated person turns nine things over in his mind. In seeing, he is bent on seeing clearly. In hearing, on hearing distinctly. In his looks, on being gentle. In his bearing, on being respectful. In his speech, on being sincere. In his work, on being careful. In doubt, on asking others. In anger, on the trouble it may bring. And when there is gain to be had, he thinks of what is right.

The wife of the ruler of a state: the ruler calls her FU ZAN, the Lady. She calls herself HSIAO T'UNG, this little child. The people of the state call her CHUN FU ZAN, our lord's Lady; to people of other states, they speak of her as K'WA HSIAO CHUN, our poor little prince. And the people of other states call her CHUN FU ZAN as well.

Confucius said: To look on what is good and reach for it as though you could never catch up; to look on what is evil and pull back from it as from scalding water — such men I have seen, and such words I have heard. To live withdrawn in order to seek out one's aims, and to do what is right in order to carry out one's principles — such words I have heard, but such men I have not seen.

Duke Ching of Ch'i had a thousand teams of four horses, yet on the day he died the people could not name a single virtue in him. Po-i and Shu-ch'i starved to death at the foot of Mount Shau-yang, and the people praise them to this day. Is this not the meaning of that old saying?

Ch'an K'ang asked Po-yu: Have you heard anything from your father that the rest of us have not? Po-yu said: No. He was once standing alone, and as I hurried across the court below the hall, he said to me, "Have you learned the Odes?" I said, "Not yet." He said, "If you do not learn the Odes, you will have nothing to converse with." So I withdrew and studied the Odes. Another day he was again standing alone, and as I hurried across the court, he said to me, "Have you learned ritual?" I said, "Not yet." He said, "If you do not learn ritual, your character can find no footing." So I withdrew and studied ritual. These two things I have heard from him. Ch'an K'ang came away delighted and said: I asked one thing and got three. I have heard about the Odes, I have heard about ritual, and I have heard that the cultivated person keeps his distance from his own son.

The wife of the ruler of a state is called by him "my lady." She calls herself "the little girl." The people of the state call her "the ruler's lady," but to those of other states they call her "our little ruler." The people of other states also call her "the ruler's lady."

Yang Ho wanted to see Confucius, and Confucius would not see him. So Ho sent him a suckling pig — and Confucius, picking an hour when Ho was out, went to his house to return thanks. But he met him on the road. Ho said to Confucius, "Come here. I want a word with you. A man hides his treasure in his coat while his country loses its way — would you call him human-hearted?" "No," said Confucius. "A man longs to serve, yet over and over lets his moment slip — would you call him wise?" "No," said Confucius. "The days and months are running out. The years do not wait for us." Confucius said, "True. I will take office."

Yang Ho wished to see Confucius, but Confucius would not go to him. So Ho sent him a gift of a suckling pig. Confucius, choosing a time when Ho was out, went to thank him for it — and met him on the road. Ho said to him: Come, let me speak with you. Then he asked: Can a man be called humane who keeps his treasure hidden in his bosom and lets his country fall into confusion? Confucius said: No. Can a man be called wise who longs to be of use in public office, and yet again and again lets the chance slip by? Confucius said: No. The days and months are passing; the years do not wait for us. Confucius said: True. I will take office.
The Master said, "By nature men are close to one another. By habit they end up far apart." The Master said, "Only two kinds never change: the wisest, and the dullest."
The Master said: By nature people are nearly alike; by practice they grow far apart.

The Master came to Wu-ch'ang and heard strings and singing all through the town. He smiled. "Why use an ox-cleaver," he said, "to kill a chicken?" Tsze-yu answered, "Master, I once heard you say, 'When the gentleman studies the Way, he loves men. When the common man studies the Way, he is easy to lead.'" The Master said, "My friends, Yen is right. What I said was a joke." Kung-shan Fu-zao, holding the city of Pi in revolt, sent for the Master, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu didn't like it. "So there is nowhere left to go," he said. "Fine. But why must it be Kung-shan?"
The Master said: It is only the wisest and the most stupid who never change.

The Master said, "Would the man have called me for nothing? If someone would only use me — could I not make an eastern Chau?" Tsze-chang asked Confucius about human-heartedness. Confucius said, "To be able to carry five things everywhere under heaven — that is human-heartedness." He asked what they were. "Gravity, generosity, good faith, diligence, kindness. Be grave, and no one will treat you with contempt. Be generous, and you will win everyone. Keep faith, and men will trust you with things. Be diligent, and you will get things done. Be kind, and you will be able to ask men for their work."

When the Master came to Wu-ch'ang, he heard the sound of strings and singing. Pleased, and smiling, he said: Why use an ox-knife to kill a chicken? Tsze-yu answered: Master, I once heard you say — when those above are taught, they love the people; when those below are taught, they are easy to govern. The Master said: My friends, Yen is right. What I said just now was only in jest.

Pi Hsi sent for him, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu said, "Master, I once heard you say, 'A gentleman does not walk into the house of a man who has chosen evil with his own hands.' Pi Hsi is holding Chung-mau in revolt. If you go to him, what will people say?" The Master said, "Yes, I said that. But don't they also say hard — so hard that grinding cannot thin it? Don't they also say white — so white that black dye cannot darken it? Am I a bitter gourd, fit to hang on a string and never be eaten?"

Kung-shan Fu-zao, holding the town of Pi in revolt, sent for the Master, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu, displeased, said: There is nowhere to go, so why must you think of going to Kung-shan? The Master said: He has not called me for nothing. If someone will use me, may I not make an eastern Chau of his domain?

The Master said, "Yu, have you heard of the six words and the six faults that shadow them?" "I have not." "Sit down, and I will tell you. To love human-heartedness without loving learning ends in folly. To love knowledge without loving learning ends in drift. To love good faith without loving learning ends in damage. To love straight speech without loving learning ends in harshness. To love courage without loving learning ends in disorder. To love firmness without loving learning ends in recklessness."

Tsze-chang asked Confucius about humaneness. Confucius said: To practice five things everywhere in the world is humaneness. He asked what they were. They are gravity, generosity, sincerity, earnestness, and kindness. Be grave, and no one will slight you. Be generous, and you will win all hearts. Be sincere, and others will trust you. Be earnest, and you will get things done. Be kind, and you will be fit to set others to work.

The Master said, "My young friends, why does none of you study the Odes? The Odes can rouse you. They can open your eyes. They can put you in company. They can teach you how to complain. Near at hand, they teach you to serve your father; further off, to serve your prince. And from them you learn the names of birds and beasts, plants and trees, more than you can count." The Master said to Po-yu, "Have you worked through the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan? A man who has not worked through the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan stands with his face against a wall."

Pi Hsi sent for him, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu said: Master, I once heard you say that the cultivated person does not keep company with a man who in his own person does evil. Pi Hsi is in revolt, holding Chung-mau; if you go to him, what will be said? The Master said: Yes, I did say that. But is it not said that what is truly hard can be ground and not worn thin? Is it not said that what is truly white can be steeped in black and not stained? Am I a bitter gourd, to be hung up and never eaten?

The Master said, "'Ritual! Ritual!' they say. Is it jade and silk they mean? 'Music! Music!' they say. Is it bells and drums?" The Master said, "A stern face over a weak heart — set that man among the small men: isn't he the thief who bores through the wall, or climbs over it?" The Master said, "The village paragon is the thief of virtue." The Master said, "To hear it on the road and tell it on the road is to throw virtue away."

The Master said: Yu, have you heard the six words and the six cloudings that go with them? Yu answered: I have not. Sit down, then, and I will tell you. To love humaneness without loving learning — the clouding is foolishness. To love knowledge without loving learning — the clouding is a mind that drifts. To love good faith without loving learning — the clouding is a harm that wounds. To love straightness without loving learning — the clouding is rudeness. To love boldness without loving learning — the clouding is rebellion. To love firmness without loving learning — the clouding is recklessness.

The Master said, "These vulgar men — can you serve a prince beside them? Before they have a thing, their one worry is getting it. Once they have it, their one worry is losing it. And a man in dread of losing his place will do anything. There is nothing he will not do." The Master said, "The ancients had three faults, and even those we may have lost. The wild men of old ignored the small things; the wild men of today just run loose. The proud men of old had sharp corners; the proud men of today have sharp tempers. The fools of old were at least straight; the fools of today are simply liars."

The Master said: My children, why do none of you study the Odes? The Odes can rouse the mind. They teach you to look into yourself. They teach you how to live with others. They teach you how to handle resentment. Near at hand, they show you how to serve your father; further off, how to serve your prince. And from them you learn the names of many birds, beasts, and plants.

The Master said, "Clever words and a charming face rarely go with human-heartedness." The Master said, "I hate purple for stealing the place of vermilion. I hate the tunes of Chang for fouling the music of the Ya. I hate the sharp-tongued for toppling states and houses." The Master said, "I would rather say nothing at all." Tsze-kung said, "But Master, if you say nothing, what will we, your students, have to pass on?" The Master said, "Does Heaven say anything? The four seasons turn, the hundred creatures are born — and does Heaven say a word?"
The Master said to Po-yu: Have you worked at the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan? A man who has not studied the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan is like one standing with his face right against a wall.

Zu Pei asked to see Confucius, and Confucius sent word that he was ill. Then, as the messenger was going out the door, he took up his lute and sang — making sure Pei heard it. Tsai Wo asked about the three years' mourning for parents. "One year is long enough," he said. "If a gentleman lets ritual alone for three years, ritual will fall apart. If he lets music alone for three years, music will collapse. Within a year the old grain is gone and the new grain is standing; the fire-drill has gone through its round of woods. A year, and mourning should end." The Master said, "A year on — eating fine rice, wearing brocade — would you be at ease?" "I would," said Wo.
The Master said: "It is ritual," they say, "it is ritual" — but are gems and silk all that ritual means? "It is music," they say, "it is music" — but are bells and drums all that music means?

"If you are at ease, then do it. A gentleman in mourning tastes no sweetness in fine food, hears no pleasure in music, finds no rest in his own house. So he does not do these things. But you are at ease — so do them." Tsai Wo went out, and the Master said, "There is no human-heartedness in Yu. A child is three years old before it leaves its parents' arms; the three years' mourning is kept everywhere under heaven. And Yu — did he not get his three years of love from his father and mother?"
The Master said: A man who puts on stern firmness while he is weak within is like one of the mean sort — like a thief who breaks through a wall, or climbs over it.

The Master said, "Stuffed with food to the end of the day, mind set on nothing — a hard case! Are there no dice players, no players of go? Even that would be better than nothing." Tsze-lu said, "Does the gentleman put courage first?" The Master said, "The gentleman puts rightness first. A great man with courage and no rightness makes a rebel. A small man with courage and no rightness makes a robber." Tsze-kung said, "Does the gentleman have his hatreds too?" The Master said, "He has his hatreds. He hates those who broadcast other men's faults. He hates the man beneath who slanders the men above. He hates courage without ritual. He hates the bold and decisive whose minds are shut."
The Master said: Your good, careful villager — the man everyone praises — is the thief of virtue.

Then the Master asked, "Ts'ze, do you have your hatreds?" Tsze-kung said, "I hate prying passed off as wisdom. I hate insolence passed off as courage. I hate informing passed off as honesty." The Master said, "Women of the house and servants are the hardest to deal with. Come close, and they lose respect. Keep back, and they resent you." The Master said, "If a man is forty and still disliked, that is how he ends."
The Master said: To pick up gossip on the road and pass it straight along is to throw your virtue away.

The Master said: These mean creatures! Can one serve a prince alongside them? Before they have gained what they want, their worry is how to get it; once they have gotten it, their worry is how not to lose it. And once they are anxious about losing it, there is nothing they will not do.

The Master said: In the old days people had three failings, which now perhaps are not even to be found. The high spirit of the ancients ran to a disregard of small things; the high spirit of today runs to wild license. The stern pride of the ancients showed as grave reserve; the stern pride of today shows as quarrelsome perversity. The simplicity of the ancients was plain straightness; the simplicity of today is sheer deceit.
The Master said: Fine words and a fawning face are seldom found together with humaneness.
The Master said: I hate the way purple robs vermilion of its luster. I hate the way the tunes of Chang corrupt the music of the Ya. I hate the way sharp tongues overthrow kingdoms and houses.

The Master said: I would rather not speak. Tsze-kung said: If you do not speak, Master, what shall we, your disciples, have to pass on? The Master said: Does Heaven speak? Yet the four seasons run their course, and all things keep being born. Does Heaven say anything?
Zu Pei wished to see Confucius. Confucius excused himself on the ground of illness. But as the messenger went out the door, the Master took up his lute and sang, so that Pei would hear him.

Tsai Wo asked about the three years' mourning for parents, saying a single year was long enough. If the cultivated person, he said, goes three years without performing the rites, the rites are sure to decay; if for three years he makes no music, music is sure to fall to ruin. In a year the old grain is used up and the new grain is in; the drill has gone through the whole round of woods for kindling fire. A year is enough. The Master said: Would you feel at ease, after only a year, eating good rice and wearing fine clothes? I would, said Wo. Then if you can feel at ease, do it. But when the cultivated person is in mourning, fine food gives him no taste, music gives him no joy, and ease of living gives him no comfort — and so he does not do as you say. But if you feel at ease, then do it. When Tsai Wo had gone out, the Master said: How inhumane Yu is! Only when a child is three years old does it leave its parents' arms. The three years' mourning is the custom of the whole world. Did Yu not have three years of his parents' love?

The Master said: Hard indeed is the man who stuffs himself with food all day and never sets his mind on anything! Are there not games of chance and chess? Even to play at those would be better than doing nothing at all.

Tsze-lu said: Does the cultivated person prize courage? The Master said: The cultivated person holds rightness highest. A man of rank with courage but no sense of right will turn to rebellion; a common man with courage but no sense of right will turn to robbery.

Tsze-kung said: Does the cultivated person too have his hatreds? The Master said: He has. He hates those who broadcast other people's faults. He hates those who, set low, slander those above them. He hates those who have courage but no regard for ritual. He hates those who are bold and headstrong but closed in their understanding. He asked: And you, Ts'ze, have you your hatreds too? I hate those who pry into things and call it wisdom. I hate those who are merely insolent and call it courage. I hate those who lay bare other people's secrets and call it straightness.
The Master said: Women and servants are the hardest to manage. Let them too close, and they grow forward; keep them at a distance, and they grow resentful.
The Master said: A man still disliked by all at forty will be so to the end.
The Viscount of Wei withdrew from the court. The Viscount of Chi became a slave to Chau. Pi-kan protested, and died for it. Confucius said, "The Yin had three human-hearted men."

The Viscount of Wei withdrew from the court. The Viscount of Chi let himself be made a slave. Pi-kan spoke out against the tyrant and was put to death. Confucius said: The Yin dynasty had three humane men.

Hui of Liu-hsia was chief judge, and three times he was thrown out of office. Someone said, "Isn't it time, sir, to leave altogether?" He said, "If I serve men by the straight Way, where can I go that they will not throw me out three times? And if I am willing to serve men by the crooked way, why should I have to leave the country of my father and mother at all?" The duke Ching of Ch'i, considering how to receive Confucius, said, "I cannot treat him as I would the head of the Chi family. I will treat him as something between Chi and Mang." Then he said, "I am old. I cannot use him." And Confucius left. The people of Ch'i sent Lu a gift of women musicians. Chi Hwan accepted them, and for three days no court was held. And Confucius left.

Hui of Liu-hsia, serving as chief judge, was dismissed from office three times. Someone said to him: Is it not time, sir, to leave this place? He answered: If I serve men in a straight way, where can I go and not be dismissed three times over? And if I would serve them in a crooked way, what need have I to leave the country of my parents?

Chieh-yu, the madman of Ch'u, went past Confucius singing: "Phoenix! Phoenix! How your virtue has withered! What is gone is past all pleading; what is coming can still be caught. Enough, enough! Danger, now, for men who meddle in government!" Confucius got down from his carriage, wanting to speak with him. But Chieh-yu quickened his step and was gone, and Confucius never got his word. Ch'ang-tsu and Chieh-ni were plowing together in the same field when Confucius passed by, and he sent Tsze-lu to ask them where the ford was. Ch'ang-tsu said, "Who is that, holding the reins?" "That is K'ung Ch'iu," said Tsze-lu. "K'ung Ch'iu of Lu?" "Yes." "Then he knows the ford."

Duke Ching of Ch'i, considering how he should treat Confucius, said: I cannot treat him as I would the head of the Chi family. I will treat him somewhere between the head of the Chi and the head of the Mang. He also said: I am old; I cannot make use of his teachings. So Confucius took his leave.

Tsze-lu asked Chieh-ni instead. "And who are you?" said Chieh-ni. "Chung Yu." "The disciple of K'ung Ch'iu of Lu?" "I am." "The whole world is one rushing flood, and who is there to change it with? You follow a master who runs from this man and that man. Wouldn't you do better following men who have run from the world itself?" And he went on raking earth over the seed without a pause. Tsze-lu went back and reported it. The Master fell quiet a moment, then said, "A man cannot flock with the birds and beasts. If I am not to live among these people — among men — whom am I to live with? If the Way held in the world, I would not be out here trying to change it."
The people of Ch'i sent Lu a gift of women musicians. Chi Hwan accepted them, and for three days no court was held. So Confucius took his leave.

Tsze-lu, traveling behind the Master, had fallen back when he met an old man carrying a weeding basket slung on his staff. Tsze-lu asked him, "Sir, have you seen my master?" The old man said, "You, whose four limbs have never worked, who couldn't tell the five grains apart — whose master?" And he planted his staff and went to weeding. Tsze-lu stood and waited, hands folded in respect. The old man kept him for the night, killed a chicken and cooked millet for him, and presented his two sons. Next day Tsze-lu caught up and told the story. The Master said, "A recluse," and sent him back to see the man again. When Tsze-lu got there, the man had gone.

Chieh-yu, the madman of Ch'u, passed by Confucius, singing: O phoenix, O phoenix, how your virtue has fallen! What is past is beyond reproof, but what is to come may yet be set right. Give it up, give it up! Those who meddle in government now walk in peril. Confucius got down from his carriage, wishing to speak with him, but the man hurried off, and he could not.

Tsze-lu said to the household, "It is not right to refuse to serve. The courtesies between old and young cannot be set aside; how then can the duty between ruler and minister be set aside? To keep his own person clean, he lets the great relation fall into ruin. A gentleman takes office because it is right to serve — knowing perfectly well that the Way is not going to prevail." The men who withdrew from the world: Po-i, Shu-ch'i, Yu-chung, I-yi, Chu-chang, Hui of Liu-hsia, Shao-lien. The Master said, "Never bending their wills, never letting their persons be shamed — that was Po-i and Shu-ch'i."

Ch'ang-tsu and Chieh-ni were ploughing together in the field when Confucius passed by, and he sent Tsze-lu to ask them where the ford was. Ch'ang-tsu said: Who is that holding the reins in the carriage? Tsze-lu said: It is K'ung Ch'iu. Is it not K'ung Ch'iu of Lu? he asked. It is, said Tsze-lu. Then he knows the ford well enough, the man said. Tsze-lu turned to Chieh-ni, who asked: And who are you, sir? I am Chung Yu, he answered. Are you not a disciple of K'ung Ch'iu of Lu? I am, said Tsze-lu. The whole world, said Chieh-ni, is flooded with disorder, and who will change it for you? Rather than follow a man who withdraws from this lord and that, would you not do better to follow those who have withdrawn from the world altogether? And he went on covering the seed without stopping. Tsze-lu went back and reported it. The Master sighed and said: I cannot herd with the birds and beasts. If I am not to live among my fellow men, then with whom? If the right way prevailed in the world, I would not be trying to change it.

"Of Hui of Liu-hsia and Shao-lien you can say they bent their wills and let their persons be shamed. But their words held the line, and their acts were what men hope for. That much, and no more. Of Yu-chung and I-yi you can say they lived hidden and said whatever they pleased. But they kept their persons clean, and their withdrawal weighed the times exactly. I am different from all of them. Nothing is ruled in for me, and nothing is ruled out." Chih, the grand music master, went to Ch'i. Kan, who played at the second meal, went to Ch'u. Liao, of the third meal, went to Ts'ai. Chueh, of the fourth, went to Ch'in. Fang-shu the drummer crossed north of the River.

Tsze-lu, following the Master, once fell behind, and met an old man carrying a basket for weeds slung from a staff on his shoulder. Tsze-lu asked him: Have you seen my master, sir? The old man said: Your four limbs have never known toil, and you cannot tell one grain from another — who is your master? And he planted his staff in the ground and went on weeding. Tsze-lu folded his hands across his breast and stood waiting. The old man kept him for the night, killed a fowl and cooked millet and fed him, and brought out his two sons to meet him. The next day Tsze-lu went on and reported it. The Master said: He is a recluse, and sent Tsze-lu back to see him again; but when he reached the place, the old man was gone. Tsze-lu said: To refuse office is not right. If the bond between old and young cannot be set aside, how can he set aside the duty between ruler and subject? Wishing to keep his own person clean, he throws that great bond into disorder. The cultivated person takes office and does the right thing it asks of him; as for the way failing to prevail, he knows that already.

Wu, who played the hand drum, crossed the Han. Yang the assistant master and Hsiang, who struck the stone chimes, crossed the sea to the islands. The duke of Chau said to his son, the duke of Lu: "A true prince does not neglect his own kin. He does not leave his great ministers bitter at never being used. He does not cast off men of the old families without grave cause. And he does not demand from any one man a talent for everything."

Those who withdrew into private life were Po-i, Shu-ch'i, Yu-chung, I-yi, Chu-chang, Hui of Liu-hsia, and Shao-lien. The Master said: Refusing to bend their wills or to suffer any stain on their persons — such, I think, were Po-i and Shu-ch'i. Of Hui of Liu-hsia and Shao-lien it may be said that they bent their wills and let their persons be stained, yet their words kept to reason and their deeds were such as men long to see; that is all there is to say of them. Of Yu-chung and I-yi it may be said that, living hidden and free in their speech, they kept their persons pure and judged well the times in giving up office. As for me, I am not like any of these: I have nothing I must do and nothing I must not do.
Chau had its eight officers: Po-ta and Po-kwo, Chung-tu and Chung-hwu, Shu-ya and Shu-hsia, Chi-sui and Chi-kwa.

Chih, the grand music master, left for Ch'i. Kan, the bandmaster of the second meal, left for Ch'u; Liao, of the third meal, for Ts'ai; Chueh, of the fourth meal, for Ch'in. Fang-shu the drummer withdrew north of the river. Wu, master of the hand-drum, withdrew to the Han. Yang, the assistant music master, and Hsiang, master of the sounding-stone, withdrew to an island in the sea.

The Duke of Chau said to his son, the Duke of Lu: The good ruler does not neglect his kin. He does not give the great ministers cause to resent being unused. Without grave reason he does not cast off the men of old families. And he does not look to find every talent in a single man.
Chau had its eight officers: Po-ta, Po-kwo, Chung-tu, Chung-hwu, Shu-ya, Shu-hsia, Chi-sui, and Chi-kwa.

Tsze-chang said, "A scholar in service who, seeing danger, will give his life; who, seeing gain, thinks of what is right; who in sacrifice thinks of reverence and in mourning thinks of grief — he will do." Tsze-chang said, "Holding virtue without breadth, trusting the Way without depth — what does such a man add to the world? And what does he take from it?"

Tsze-chang said: A man of office who, seeing danger, is ready to give his life; who, offered gain, thinks of what is right; who in sacrifice thinks of reverence, and in mourning thinks of grief — such a man will do.

The disciples of Tsze-hsia asked Tsze-chang about making friends. Tsze-chang said, "What does Tsze-hsia tell you?" They answered, "Tsze-hsia says: keep company with those who are worth it, and turn away those who are not." Tsze-chang said, "That is not what I was taught. A gentleman honors the worthy and makes room for the many; he praises the good and pities the incapable. If I am greatly worthy, who is there I cannot make room for? If I am unworthy, men will turn me away first — how would I ever get to turning away them?" Tsze-hsia said, "Even the minor paths have things worth seeing along them. But follow them far and you bog down — which is why the gentleman does not take them."
Tsze-chang said: To hold to virtue but not to enlarge it, to believe in the Way but not firmly — what does it matter whether such a man exists or not?

Tsze-hsia said, "A man who learns, day by day, what he still lacks, and month by month does not lose what he has — call him a lover of learning." Tsze-hsia said, "Study widely and hold your purpose fast; question closely and think about what is near at hand. Human-heartedness is in that." Tsze-hsia said, "The hundred craftsmen live in their shops to finish their work. The gentleman learns, to carry his Way to its end."

The disciples of Tsze-hsia asked Tsze-chang about how to deal with others. Tsze-chang said: What does Tsze-hsia tell you? They answered: Tsze-hsia says, "Keep company with those worth keeping, and turn away those who are not." Tsze-chang said: That is not what I learned. The cultivated person honors the worthy and makes room for all; he praises the good and pities the weak. Am I a man of great worth? Then whom could I not bear with? Am I a man of no worth? Then others will turn away from me — what business have I turning away from them?

Tsze-hsia said, "The small man always dresses up his faults." Tsze-hsia said, "The gentleman changes three times. From far off he looks stern. Up close, he is warm. And when you hear him speak, every word is exact." Tsze-hsia said, "The gentleman wins his people's trust, and then he puts them to work; without the trust, they would call it oppression. He wins his prince's trust, and then he criticizes; without the trust, the prince would call it slander." Tsze-hsia said, "In the great virtues a man must not cross the line. In the small ones, a little coming and going is allowed."
Tsze-hsia said: Even in the lesser arts and crafts there is something worth seeing; but follow them too far and you risk getting mired. That is why the cultivated person does not take them up.

Tsze-yu said, "The students of Tsze-hsia can sprinkle and sweep a floor, answer a call, come forward and step back — and do it well. But those are twigs. Of the root they know nothing. What sort of learning is that?" Tsze-hsia heard it and said, "Ah, Yen Yu is wrong. In the gentleman's Way, which lesson do you hand on first? Which do you leave to ripen? Students are like plants: you tend each kind as its kind requires. The gentleman's Way does not cheat its beginners. And to hold it whole, first things and last things in a single grasp — only the sage does that."
Tsze-hsia said: A man who notices each day what he still lacks, and month by month does not forget what he has gained — he may be said to love learning indeed.

Tsze-hsia said, "Strength left over from office should go to learning. Strength left over from learning should go to office." Tsze-hsia said, "Mourning should go all the way to grief, and stop there." Tsze-hsia said, "My friend Chang can do what other men find nearly impossible. Even so, he is not yet human-hearted." Master Tsang said, "How grand Chang is! Hard to work at human-heartedness beside a man like that." Master Tsang said, "I heard this from the Master: no man ever gives the whole of himself — unless it is in mourning his parents."
Tsze-hsia said: Learn widely and hold firmly to your purpose, inquire earnestly and reflect on what lies near at hand — humaneness is there.

Master Tsang said, "I heard this from the Master: the filial piety of Mang Chwang — in most of it, other men could match him. But he changed nothing: his father's ministers, his father's way of governing, he kept them all. That is the part hard to match." The head of the Mang family made Yang Fu a criminal judge, and Yang Fu came to Master Tsang for advice. Tsang said, "The men above have lost the Way, and the people have come apart — and it has been so for a long time. When you dig out the truth of a case, grieve for them and pity them. Never congratulate yourself on finding it."
Tsze-hsia said: The artisans stay in their shops to get their work done; the cultivated person learns to reach the Way.

Tsze-kung said, "Chau cannot have been as wicked as his name. This is why a gentleman hates to live downstream: everything foul in the world comes washing down to him." Tsze-kung said, "The faults of a gentleman are eclipses of the sun and moon. When he fails, everyone sees it. When he mends it, everyone looks up again." Kung-sun Ch'ao of Wei asked Tsze-kung, "Where did Chung-ni get his learning?" Tsze-kung said, "The Way of Wan and Wu has not fallen to the ground yet. It is alive in people. The worthy remember its great parts; the rest remember its small ones. Nobody is without a piece of the Way of Wan and Wu. Where could our Master go and not be learning? And why should he have needed one fixed teacher?"
Tsze-hsia said: The small man is sure to gloss over his faults.

Shu-sun Wu-shu said to the great officers at court, "Tsze-kung is a better man than Chung-ni." Tsze-fu Ching-po repeated it to Tsze-kung, who said, "Put it in terms of a house and its wall. My wall comes up to a man's shoulder: anyone walking by can look over and see whatever is good inside. The Master's wall is many fathoms high: unless you find the gate and enter, you will never see the beauty of the ancestral temple or the hundred officers in their splendor. And the ones who find the gate, I think, are few. So the chief's remark — what else would you expect?"
Tsze-hsia said: The cultivated person shows three faces. Seen from afar, he is grave; come close, and he is mild; hear him speak, and his words are firm.

Shu-sun Wu-shu spoke against Chung-ni. Tsze-kung said, "Save your breath. Chung-ni cannot be pulled down. The worth of other men is a hill, a mound — a thing you can still climb over. Chung-ni is the sun and the moon. There is no climbing over them. A man may choose to shut them out, but what harm does that do the sun and the moon? It only shows how badly he has measured himself." Ch'an Tsze-ch'in said to Tsze-kung, "You are being modest. In what way is Chung-ni better than you?" Tsze-kung said, "One word can mark a gentleman wise, and one word can mark him a fool. We cannot afford to be careless in what we say. No one reaches the Master, the way no one climbs a stairway to the sky."

Tsze-hsia said: The cultivated person must win his people's trust before he sets them to labor; without that trust, they will think he is grinding them down. He must win his ruler's trust before he remonstrates; without that trust, the ruler will think he is slandering him.
