"Had the Master been given a state or a great house, it would have gone as the old words say. He plants the people, and they stand. He leads them, and they walk. He settles them, and they come from every side. He stirs them, and they move as one. Living, he is their glory. Dead, he is their grief. How could anyone reach him?"
Tsze-hsia said: So long as a man does not cross the line in the great virtues, he may come and go a little in the small ones.

Tsze-yu said: The young followers of Tsze-hsia can sprinkle and sweep, answer when spoken to, and come and go properly enough; but these are only the branches — they are left ignorant of the root. What is to be made of that? Tsze-hsia heard it and said: Ah, Yen Yu is wrong. In teaching the Way, what is to be handed on first, and what set aside as later? Disciples are like plants, sorted by their kinds. How could the Way of the cultivated person play them false? It is the sage alone who holds the beginning and the end of learning in one.
Tsze-hsia said: The officer who has discharged his duties should give his spare hours to learning; the student who has finished his learning should give himself to office.
Tsze-hsia said: In mourning, let grief reach its full measure and stop there.
Tsze-hsia said: My friend Chang can do what is hard to do — but he is not yet humane.
Master Tsang said: How lofty Chang is! Yet it is hard to practice humaneness alongside him.
Master Tsang said: I heard this from the Master — a man may not show all that is in him, but he is sure to show it in mourning for his parents.

Master Tsang said: I heard this from the Master — the filial devotion of Mang Chwang was such as other men could match in most things; but that he did not change his father's ministers or his father's ways of government — that is hard to match.

When the head of the Mang family made Yang Fu chief judge, Yang Fu went to Master Tsang. Master Tsang said: Those above have lost their way, and the people have long been scattered. When you uncover the truth of a case, grieve for them and have pity — do not be glad of your own skill.
Tsze-kung said: Chau's wickedness was not so great as they make it out. This is why the cultivated person hates to dwell downstream, where all the foulness of the world comes flowing in upon him.
Tsze-kung said: The faults of the cultivated person are like an eclipse of the sun or the moon. When he errs, every man sees it; when he sets it right, every man looks up to him.

Kung-sun Ch'ao of Wei asked Tsze-kung: From whom did Chung-ni learn? Tsze-kung said: The Way of Wan and Wu has not fallen to the ground; it lives on among men. The worthy remember its greater parts, lesser men its smaller parts — there is no man who has not some of the Way of Wan and Wu in him. Where could the Master go and not learn? And what need had he of one fixed teacher?

Shu-sun Wu-shu said to the great officers at court: Tsze-kung is greater than Chung-ni. Tsze-fu Ching-po told this to Tsze-kung, who said: Take the comparison of a house and its wall. My wall reaches only to the shoulders, so one can peep over it and see the fine things within. But my Master's wall is many fathoms high. Unless you find the gate and go in, you will never see the ancestral temple in its beauty, nor the throng of officers in their splendor. And few, it may be, find the gate. Was the gentleman's remark not just what one would expect?

Shu-sun Wu-shu spoke ill of Chung-ni. Tsze-kung said: It is no use. Chung-ni cannot be slandered. The worth of other men is hills and mounds, which one can step over; Chung-ni is the sun and the moon, which no one can step over. Though a man should wish to cut himself off from them, what harm does he do to the sun and the moon? He only shows that he does not know his own measure.

Ch'an Tsze-ch'in said to Tsze-kung: You are too modest. How can Chung-ni be greater than you? Tsze-kung said: By a single word a man may be judged wise, and by a single word judged foolish — so we should be careful what we say. The Master cannot be reached, as the sky cannot be climbed by a stair. Had the Master been given a state or a great house to rule, then — as the saying goes — he would have raised the people up, and they would have stood; led them on, and they would have followed; given them peace, and they would have come to him; stirred them, and they would have lived in harmony. In life he was glorious; in death he was bitterly mourned. How could such a man be reached?

sections.label: Book XX
sections.title: Yao Said
The Charge of the Ancient Kings, and How to Govern

segments.text: Yao said, "Ah, Shun. The count of Heaven's succession rests now on your shoulders. Hold honestly to the center. If the four seas fall into hardship and want, Heaven's gift ends forever." Shun laid the same charge on Yu. T'ang said, "I, the little child Li, dare to offer this dark bull, and dare to declare it plainly to you, most august and sovereign Lord: the guilty I dare not pardon; your servants I do not hide from you. The judging of them is in your own heart, Lord. If there is guilt in me, let it not touch the ten thousand regions. If there is guilt in the ten thousand regions, let it rest on me."

Yao said: "Oh, Shun! The succession that Heaven appoints now rests in your person. Hold faithfully to the due Mean. If the people within the four seas fall into want, Heaven's gift to you will end forever." Shun, in his turn, charged Yu with the same words. T'ang said: "I, the child Li, dare to offer a dark victim, and dare to make this known to you, most great and sovereign God: the guilty I dare not pardon, and your ministers, O God, I do not keep hidden; the judging of them is in your mind. If I myself offend, let it not be charged against the people of the myriad regions; if the people of the myriad regions offend, let the offense rest on me alone." Chau bestowed great gifts, and the good were made rich. "Though he has his own kinsmen, they are not the equal of my humane men. If the people do wrong, let the blame fall on me, the One Man." He saw carefully to the weights and measures, reviewed the body of the laws, restored the offices that had been abolished, and good government ran through the kingdom. He revived states that had been wiped out, raised up families whose line had been broken, and called back to office those who had withdrawn into obscurity; and the hearts of the people throughout the kingdom turned to him. What he held chief were these: the food of the people, the rites of mourning, and the sacrifices. By his generosity he won them all; by his good faith the people came to trust him; by his diligence his work was great; by his fairness all were glad.

Chau gave great gifts, and good men grew rich. "I have kinsmen of my own," said the king, "but better than kinsmen are human-hearted men. If the hundred families do wrong, let it lie on me — the One Man." He set the weights and measures right, went over the laws again, restored the officers who had been dismissed — and government flowed through the whole kingdom. He raised up states that had been wiped out, mended lines of succession that had been cut, called back to office men who had gone into hiding — and the hearts of everyone under heaven turned to him. What he gave most weight to: the people's food, mourning, and sacrifice. He was generous, and won the crowd. He kept faith, and the people leaned on him. He was diligent, and the work was done. He was just, and they were glad.

Tsze-chang asked Confucius: "How should one in authority act, so as to govern well?" The Master said: "Let him honor the five excellent things and cast out the four bad things; then he may govern well." Tsze-chang asked: "What are the five excellent things?" The Master said: "That in authority he is generous without wastefulness; that he sets the people to work without their resenting it; that he wants things without greed; that he keeps his dignity without pride; that he is commanding without fierceness." Tsze-chang asked: "What is it to be generous without wastefulness?" The Master said: "To make more profitable to the people the very things they already profit from — is that not to be generous without wastefulness? To choose the labors that are fitting, and set them to those — then who will resent it? To set one's desire on humane government, and secure it — who will call that greed? Whether his people are many or few, his affairs great or small, he never dares to slight them — is that not dignity without pride? He sets his robe and cap straight and gives his look a gravity, so that men regard him with awe — is that not to be commanding without fierceness?" Tsze-chang asked: "What are the four bad things?" The Master said: "To put men to death without having taught them — that is cruelty. To demand the work finished without having warned them — that is tyranny. To be slack in giving the orders, then strict when the deadline comes — that is injury. And in giving men what is due to them, to be stingy in the handing out — that is the part of a petty clerk."

Tsze-chang asked Confucius, "What must a man do, to be fit to govern?" The Master said, "Honor the five fine things, and cast out the four ugly things. Then he is fit to govern." Tsze-chang said, "What are the five fine things?" The Master said, "The gentleman in authority is generous without expense. He works the people, and they do not resent it. He desires, and is not greedy. He is at his ease, and is not proud. He is imposing, and never fierce."

Tsze-chang said, "What is 'generous without expense'?" The Master said, "Benefit the people by way of the things that already benefit them — generous, is it not, and at no expense? Choose the labors that are rightly theirs and set them to work — who resents that? Desire human-heartedness, and obtain human-heartedness — where is the greed in that? Many or few, great or small, the gentleman never dares to brush a man aside — at ease, is he not, and never proud? He sets his robe and cap straight and lifts a level gaze, and men look at him with awe — imposing, is he not, and never fierce?" Tsze-chang said, "And the four ugly things?" The Master said, "To execute people without ever teaching them — that is called cruelty. To demand the finished count without fair warning — that is called tyranny. To let an order lie slack and then insist on it to the day — that is called laying a trap."

"And when a thing must be given to men in any case, to count it out grudgingly — that is called playing the petty clerk." The Master said, "A man who does not know Heaven's decree has no way to be a gentleman. A man who does not know ritual has no way to stand. A man who does not know words has no way to know men."

The Master said: Without knowing the ordinances of Heaven, it is impossible to be a cultivated person. Without knowing ritual, it is impossible to take one's stand. Without knowing words, it is impossible to know people.
